core.definition: Relating to scientism, the view that science alone gives real knowledge and can answer every important question. Usually used critically.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the third-from-last syllable, -TIS-. The first two syllables are reduced, so 'sci-en' sounds like 'sy-un', not 'see-en'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. The word usually criticizes someone for claiming that science can settle questions outside its proper scope, such as ethics or meaning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in philosophy, theology, and debates about science and religion, not in casual talk. Saying 'That's a scientistic view' signals disagreement, so use it with care. It is not a compliment, unlike 'scientific', which describes sound method.

distinctions.note: Scientific describes rigorous method and evidence; scientistic criticizes the belief that science is the only valid source of knowledge.
A scientist is a person who does science; scientistic describes an attitude or claim, not a person's job.

examples.everyday: My brother-in-law thinks every question about marriage has a lab answer, which I find a little scientistic.
examples.professional: The draft memo's scientistic framing assumes that the data alone can settle policy trade-offs, and it leaves out stakeholder values.
examples.analytical: A scientistic account of consciousness treats subjective experience as irrelevant until it can be measured, and so it changes the question instead of answering it.

nuance.analogy: A scientistic view is like a carpenter who sees every problem as a nail and reaches for the hammer every time.
nuance.etymology: From scientism, from Latin scientia 'knowledge', with the adjective suffix -istic.
common_mistakes: Using it as praise; it usually criticizes and is not a synonym for 'scientific'.
Stressing the wrong syllable; the stress is on -TIS-, not on the first syllable.

senses.definition: Very hot.
senses.example: It was a scorching summer, and the ice-cream sellers plied a roaring trade.

senses.definition: Bitterly sarcastic; scathing; withering.
senses.example: Her scorching review of the restaurant called the food bland and the service insulting.

senses.definition: Sexy, sexual, attractive.
Of speed when driving, running, etc.: Very high.
senses.example: He was clocked doing scorching speeds on the freeway, well over a hundred miles per hour.

senses.definition: The act or result of something being scorched.
senses.example: The scorching on the lawn after the fertilizer spill was visible for weeks.

core.definition: Extremely hot, often describing weather or the sun; in some contexts, bitterly harsh criticism or, informally, sexually attractive.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SKOR, and the final -ing is a light, short vowel, not a long 'eeng'. The 'r' is strong in American speech, so pronounce it clearly.

nuance.connotation: Negative in the weather sense (uncomfortably hot). In criticism it is harsh and negative, and in the attractiveness sense it is informal and positive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'scorching hot' or 'scorching summer' for very intense heat, especially on the news or in weather talk. Using it for sarcastic criticism sounds sharp and literary. The sense of sexually attractive is informal slang, so avoid it in professional settings. A natural reply to 'It's scorching today!' is 'Let's get some iced tea.'

distinctions.note: Hot is neutral and everyday; scorching is much stronger and suggests that the heat is painful or dangerous.
Sweltering suggests heavy, humid, oppressive heat; scorching suggests dry, intense, burning heat.
Scathing is the usual word for harsh criticism; scorching is less common in that sense and sounds more literary.

examples.everyday: It is scorching out there, so bring water if you are going to the park.
examples.professional: The reviewer gave the report a scorching critique, pointing out every gap in the data.
examples.analytical: The essay offers a scorching critique of the argument, exposing its reliance on unexamined assumptions.

nuance.analogy: A scorching day is like standing next to an open oven: the heat is so intense that it feels like it is pressing on you.
nuance.etymology: From scorch (verb) plus the adjective-forming -ing.
common_mistakes: Using scorching for mild warmth; it means intense heat, so 'scorching' is too strong for a pleasant day.
Using the attractiveness sense in formal or work conversation, where it can sound inappropriate.

conversation.text: It's scorching outside; let's stay in the pool.
It was a scorching day, over a hundred degrees.
The sand was scorching, so we ran to the water.

senses.definition: A device that has a helical function.
senses.example: The jar lid was stuck, so I wrapped a towel around it to get a better grip on the screw.

senses.definition: A simple machine, a helical inclined plane.
senses.example: Physics class taught us that a screw is an inclined plane wrapped around a cylinder.

senses.definition: A (usually) metal fastener consisting of a partially or completely threaded shank, sometimes with a threaded point, and a head used to both hold the top material and to drive the screw either directly into a soft material or into a prepared hole.
senses.example: I drove a short wood screw into the stud to hang the shelf.

senses.definition: An Archimedes screw.
senses.example: The farm used an Archimedes screw to lift irrigation water up the hillside.

senses.definition: A steam vessel propelled by a screw instead of wheels.
senses.example: The old steam screw carried coal and cotton up the river to Memphis.

senses.definition: The motion of screwing something; a turn or twist to one side.
senses.example: Give the lid one more screw to the left and it should seal.

senses.definition: A prison guard.
senses.example: The screw walked the cellblock at midnight, rattling his keys against the bars.

senses.definition: An extortioner; a sharp bargainer; a skinflint.
senses.example: Our landlord is such a screw that he charges for every late minute.

senses.definition: Sexual intercourse; the act of screwing.
senses.example: He bragged that he'd had a screw, but his friends didn't believe him.

senses.definition: A casual sexual partner.
senses.example: She told her roommate the guy from the bar was just a screw, nothing serious.

senses.definition: Backspin.
senses.example: He put screw on the cue ball so it would come back toward him.

senses.definition: A straight line in space with which a definite linear magnitude termed the pitch is associated. It is used to express the displacement of a rigid body, which may always be made to consist of a rotation about an axis combined with a translation parallel to that axis.
senses.example: In rigid body mechanics, a screw combines a rotation about an axis with a translation along it.

senses.definition: An amphipod crustacean.
senses.example: the skeleton screw (Caprella)

senses.definition: Rheumatism.
senses.example: Grandpa blamed his stiff knees on the screw every time the weather turned cold.

senses.definition: A ship's propeller.
senses.example: The ferry's screw churned up mud when it backed away from the dock.

senses.definition: An instructor who examines with great or unnecessary severity; also, a searching or strict examination of a student by an instructor.
senses.example: Professor Hale was a screw who graded every essay with brutal severity.

senses.definition: (dated) A twist of paper, especially one containing a small quantity of a material such as salt or tobacco.
senses.example: Before potato crisps were sold pre-salted each packet would contain a screw of salt.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: (dated) An old, worn-out, unsound and worthless horse.
senses.example: The farmer sold the old screw for dog food after it went lame.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: To connect or assemble pieces using a screw.
To have sexual intercourse with.
To cheat someone or ruin their chances in a game or other situation.
To extort or practice extortion upon; to oppress by unreasonable or extortionate exactions; to put the screws on.
To contort.
To miskick (a ball) by hitting it with the wrong part of the foot.
To screw back.
Used to express great displeasure with, or contemptuous dismissal of, someone or something. To give up on, to abandon, delay, to not think about someone or something.
senses.example: Screw those jerks, and screw their stupid rules!

senses.definition: To examine (a student) rigidly; to subject to a severe examination.
To leave; to go away; to scram.

core.definition: A metal fastener with a spiral ridge that is turned, not hammered, to hold pieces together or to fix something to a surface.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a long oo vowel like 'too'. Keep the r right after the k, and do not insert a vowel between sk and r.

nuance.connotation: Neutral for the hardware sense. Some other senses are vulgar or rude, and 'screwed' in the sense of ruined is informal and negative.
nuance.usage_note: The fastener sense is everyday talk in American hardware stores: 'Do you have a three-quarter-inch wood screw?' Avoid the vulgar sexual sense and never say 'screw you' casually, since it sounds very rude. 'Screw up' means make a mistake, and 'I'm screwed' means I'm in serious trouble, both informal.

distinctions.note: A bolt usually passes through a hole and is held by a nut, while a screw is turned into the material itself or into a threaded hole.
A nail is driven straight in without turning, while a screw is turned in and can be removed without damage.

examples.everyday: Can you hand me that screw from the drawer so I can fix the cabinet door?
examples.professional: The assembly spec calls for a torque-controlled screw at each bracket to keep the tolerance.
examples.analytical: Like a screw, a long argument tightens its grip with each turn, drawing the premises closer to the conclusion.

nuance.analogy: A screw is an inclined plane wrapped around a rod, so turning it converts rotation into steady pulling force.
nuance.etymology: Middle English scrue, from a Middle Dutch or Old French source; exact origin uncertain.
common_mistakes: Using 'screw' in the vulgar sexual sense or 'screw you' in polite conversation, where it sounds offensive.
Saying a long 'skrew' with a diphthong; the vowel is a pure long oo.

screw.etymology: From Middle English *screw*, *scrue* (“screw”); apparently, despite the difference in meaning, from Old French *escroue* (“nut, cylindrical socket, screwhole”), from Latin *scrōfa* (“female pig”) through comparison with the corkscrew shape of a pig's penis.

senses.definition: The state or condition of being scrumptious.

core.definition: The quality of being extremely delicious, delightful, or appealing, especially when describing food or treats.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SKRUM. The ending -ness is a reduced 'nuhs', with no separate vowel like 'ness' in 'Nessie'.

nuance.connotation: Positive and playful. It praises an appealing quality, often with a humorous or enthusiastic tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use scrumptiousness in conversation, where they say 'the food was scrumptious' instead. The noun appears mostly in food writing, reviews, or humorous writing. A natural reply to praise is 'Thanks, I'm glad you liked it.'

distinctions.note: Deliciousness is the everyday word for good taste, while scrumptiousness is more playful and stresses delight and appeal.
Appeal is general attractiveness, while scrumptiousness is specifically about things that seem good enough to eat.

examples.everyday: I can't get over the scrumptiousness of this pie, so tell me your secret.
examples.professional: The brand guide praises the scrumptiousness of the packaging, but the product copy needs to explain what is inside.
examples.analytical: Critics often confuse the scrumptiousness of a dish with its nutritional value, though the two qualities are independent.

nuance.analogy: Like a dessert that makes a small celebration out of every bite.
nuance.etymology: From scrumptious, of uncertain origin, plus the suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Using the noun in everyday talk; in speech Americans prefer the adjective scrumptious.
Stressing the last syllable instead of the first, SKRUM.

senses.definition: A person who is employed to provide security for people or property.

core.definition: A person employed to watch over people or property, such as a building, store or event.

pronunciation.tip: In this compound, 'GUARD' gets the strongest stress, while 'security' keeps its own main stress on KYUR. Americans say the 'r' in 'guard' clearly, so it is not 'gard' with a short vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a job, though some people may feel a slight distance or suspicion toward guards in stores or buildings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'security guard' for people who work at buildings, malls, hospitals and events, usually employed by a private company. The phrase is common in everyday speech and in job listings. For a police officer, use 'police officer' instead, because guards generally cannot make arrests.

distinctions.note: The two terms are nearly identical, though 'security officer' is somewhat more common in corporate and government settings.
A police officer enforces the law and can make arrests, while a security guard usually only observes, reports and deters problems.

collocations: on duty as a security guard

examples.everyday: The security guard at the mall asked me to show my receipt before I left the store.
examples.professional: We hired a security guard company to cover the building entrance after business hours.
examples.analytical: The security guard's function is preventive: observing, deterring and reporting, rather than enforcing the law.

nuance.analogy: A security guard is like a lighthouse keeper: they watch the area, warn of trouble, and call for help rather than fighting the storm themselves.
nuance.etymology: From 'security' (from Latin securitas, 'freedom from care') and 'guard' (from Old French garder, 'to watch over').
common_mistakes: Saying 'security guardian' or 'security man' when most Americans use 'security guard'
Stressing 'security' on the last syllable or failing to give 'guard' the main stress

senses.definition: Having or made of segments.

core.definition: Divided into separate parts or sections; made of distinct segments that fit together.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The -ed ending is pronounced /ɪd/ because it follows t, so say 'tid'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and descriptive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use segmented for things like a market divided into groups, a multi-part process, or an orange that separates into slices. In business and data work it often describes customers grouped into categories. Casual speakers might say 'divided into sections' instead.

distinctions.note: Divided is general and everyday; segmented suggests clear, often regular parts.
Modular emphasizes parts that can be used or replaced independently; segmented only means split into parts.

examples.everyday: The orange came apart into neat, segmented slices, and the kids loved it.
examples.professional: We need a segmented view of churn by region and plan type before the board meeting.
examples.analytical: The argument presupposes a segmented model of the self, in which reason and desire occupy separate compartments.

nuance.analogy: Like a chocolate bar with clear squares you can snap apart.
nuance.etymology: From segment, from Latin segmentum, plus the adjective ending -ed.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing -ed as /d/ or /t/ rather than /ɪd/.
Using segmented for stacked levels; layered is the better word for that.

senses.definition: The conscious control of one's own behavior.

core.definition: The conscious control of your own feelings and behavior, especially when you are tempted, angry or under pressure.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MAND, the second syllable of 'command', and the first syllable 'kuh' is a weak schwa. Do not say 'ko-MAND' with an oh sound; the vowel in 'command' is the short a of 'hand'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises calm, disciplined control over one's reactions.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely say self-command in everyday speech; they say 'self-control' or 'self-discipline'. You will see it in older books, formal essays, moral philosophy and some sermons. If you use it in conversation, it may sound stiff or literary, so 'she kept her cool' or 'she had great self-control' is more natural.

distinctions.note: Self-control is the everyday American term for the same idea, and it is far more common in conversation and writing.
Self-discipline stresses steady effort over time to reach a goal, such as exercising daily, while self-command often describes control in a single moment.
Composure is an outward calm that others can see, while self-command is the inner control that produces it.

examples.everyday: Even when the waiter brought the wrong order, she kept her self-command and just smiled.
examples.professional: Under heavy pressure from the client, the manager showed admirable self-command and kept the meeting on track.
examples.analytical: Aristotle treats enkrateia, often translated as self-control or self-command, as a state in which reason governs appetite.

nuance.analogy: Like a rudder that steers a boat through rough water, keeping it on course when the waves push against it.
nuance.etymology: From self- plus command, from Old French comander, from Latin commendare, 'to entrust'.
common_mistakes: Using self-command in everyday conversation where 'self-control' sounds more natural.
Confusing it with 'commandment', which is a rule given by God or an authority.
Pronouncing the second syllable with an oh vowel, as in 'ko-MOND'.
nuance.biblical_note: In the RSV, self-control is the usual rendering of the Greek word enkrateia, meaning mastery over one's desires. Galatians 5:22-23 lists self-control as a fruit of the Spirit, alongside love and joy. In 1 Corinthians 9:25 (RSV) Paul compares the Christian life to an athlete who exercises self-control in all things, aiming at an imperishable crown.

senses.definition: The awareness of the self as an entity.
senses.example: Philosophers have long debated whether self-consciousness is necessary for moral responsibility and free will.

senses.definition: Shyness; a feeling of unease in social situations.
senses.example: Her self-consciousness made the first day at the new school feel like an endless ordeal.

core.definition: A feeling of unease or embarrassment about being watched, judged or noticed by other people.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on KAHN, the first syllable of 'conscious', and the -ness ending is a reduced 'nus'. Say the sh sound clearly in the middle, not 'see-us'.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral. It describes a feeling of discomfort, though some people see it as a sign of thoughtfulness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use self-consciousness in everyday talk about teenagers, public speaking, body image, or accents. In philosophy and psychology, it can also mean awareness of oneself as a thinking being. In casual conversation, people often say 'I was so self-conscious' rather than using the noun.

distinctions.note: Shyness is a general personality of quiet reserve, while self-consciousness is a feeling about being watched in a particular moment.
Embarrassment is a sudden feeling after a specific event, while self-consciousness can last and affect everything you do in public.
Self-awareness means understanding your strengths, weaknesses and emotions, and it is usually positive, while self-consciousness is about fear of judgment.

examples.everyday: I felt a wave of self-consciousness when everyone turned around to look at me on stage.
examples.professional: Try not to let self-consciousness stop you from speaking up in meetings, since your question may help others too.
examples.analytical: Descartes' cogito points to a self-consciousness prior to social judgment, though later philosophers debated whether the self can know itself without others.

nuance.analogy: Like a spotlight that suddenly turns onto you, making every movement feel visible and possibly awkward.
nuance.etymology: From self- plus consciousness; conscious comes from Latin conscius, 'knowing with oneself'.
common_mistakes: Using self-consciousness as an adjective; the adjective is self-conscious.
Confusing shyness with self-consciousness; you can be outgoing and still feel self-conscious.
Stressing the second syllable of the word 'conscious' instead of KAHN.
nuance.biblical_note: Genesis 3:7 (RSV) describes the moment after the first humans eat the fruit, when their eyes are opened and they know they are naked. Their sudden awareness of themselves and of being seen leads them to cover themselves. Many readers see here the origin of shame and self-conscious hiding.

senses.definition: An act of self-refuting.
senses.example: His self-refutation was obvious when he argued against the very policy he had written.

core.definition: The act of disproving your own statement or argument, usually by showing that it contradicts itself.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on TAY in ref-yoo-TAY-shuhn, while ref keeps a lighter secondary stress. Non-native speakers often stress YOO or the first syllable instead, so keep ref short like the start of reference.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in logic and philosophy, but calling an argument self-refuting is a sharp criticism of the argument.
nuance.usage_note: This word is used mainly in philosophy, logic, debate and academic writing, not in everyday talk. Americans would more often say 'he contradicted himself' or 'the argument undermines itself' in casual conversation. Calling an argument self-refuting is precise only when you can show exactly where the statement disproves its own truth.

distinctions.note: Self-contradiction means asserting two incompatible claims, while self-refutation is stronger: the statement, if true, shows itself to be false, as in saying I cannot speak a word of English while speaking English.
Inconsistency is a general mismatch between claims, while self-refutation is a particular kind in which a claim undermines its own truth.
Refutation is any disproof, usually by an outside party, while self-refutation is when an argument disproves itself.

examples.everyday: Saying nobody can really know anything is kind of self-refutation, isn't it?
examples.professional: The draft's claim that all metrics are meaningless is self-refutation, since the paper relies on those metrics to reach its conclusion.
examples.analytical: The objection that radical skepticism commits self-refutation is old: if nothing can be known, then the claim that nothing can be known is itself unknown.

nuance.analogy: A sign reading Do not believe anything you read is self-refuting: it asks you to believe the very sign you are reading.
nuance.etymology: Self- plus refutation, from Latin refutatio, from refutare, 'to repel or drive back'.
common_mistakes: Confusing refutation with refusal, which means declining to do something
Using self-refutation for ordinary contradictions, when it specifically means the statement disproves itself
Stressing YOO or the first syllable instead of TAY in ref-yoo-TAY-shun

senses.definition: NATO & ICAO radiotelephony clear code (spelling-alphabet name) for the digit 7.
senses.example: On the radio, the pilot read the tail number, saying Niner and Seven clearly.

senses.definition: The digit/figure 7 or an occurrence thereof.
senses.example: He wrote three sevens on the paper.

senses.definition: A card bearing seven pips.
senses.example: He dealt the seven, then tossed the rest of his hand onto the table.

senses.definition: The soft drink 7 Up.
senses.example: a whisky and seven

core.definition: The number 7, one more than six, written as 7.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a reduced vowel with a syllabic n, so it sounds like 'SEV-n'. Do not make the second syllable a full 'ehn' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a basic number with cultural associations, such as lucky seven.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say seven in everyday talk for times, ages, prices, and counts. When spelling numbers on the phone or radio, Americans sometimes use the alphabet name for 7, but in ordinary conversation simply say 'seven.' Note that the teen form seventeen has stress on the second syllable, which is a common mistake.

distinctions.note: Seventeen stresses the second syllable (sev-en-TEEN), while seven stresses the first syllable (SEV-en), so the two are easy to confuse in speech.
Seventh is the ordinal form for the position 7th, while seven is the cardinal number for the count 7.

examples.everyday: The store closes at seven, so let's leave by six thirty.
examples.professional: The model retrains every seven days, which is enough for our current data volume.
examples.analytical: Of the integers from one to seven, exactly four are prime.

nuance.analogy: Like a combination lock that opens only on the right number, seven is a single fixed value that stands apart from its neighbors.
nuance.etymology: From Old English seofon, from Proto-Germanic *sebun.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable of seven, which makes it sound like seventeen.
Confusing the cardinal seven with the ordinal seventh in dates, such as writing 'the seven of May' instead of 'the seventh of May'.
nuance.biblical_note: In Hebrew the number seven is sheva (שֶׁבַע), and it carries symbolic weight as a number of completeness. Genesis 2:2 (RSV) says that God finished his work on the seventh day and rested, which makes the seventh day a pattern for the Sabbath. Revelation 1:20 (RSV) explains that the seven stars are the angels of the seven churches, where seven signifies the whole church addressed in that book.

seven.etymology: From Middle English *seven*, from Old English *seofon* (“seven”), from **sebun* (“seven”), from Proto-Germanic **sebun* (“seven”), from Proto-Indo-European **septḿ̥* (“seven”).

senses.definition: Without sexual activity.
senses.example: They have a sexless marriage.

senses.definition: Without physical or behavioral sexual distinction.
senses.example: The sexless workers in the colony forage for food and guard the hive entrance.

senses.definition: Provoking or showing no sexual desire.
senses.example: A small child is sexless.

senses.definition: Without sex appeal. (Can we add an example for this sense?)
senses.example: The hotel lobby was sexless, with beige walls and generic furniture everywhere.

core.definition: Having no sexual activity or sexual desire, especially in a relationship or marriage.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The ks-l cluster is said quickly, so do not add a vowel between the k and the l.

nuance.connotation: Negative to neutral. It often describes a relationship as sad or lacking intimacy, and it can sound unkind if used about a person.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sexless mostly to describe relationships, marriages or dating lives in personal or media contexts. Saying someone is sexless can sound judgmental, so for a neutral description use not sexually active or single. Celibate is the better word for a person who chooses not to have sex, often for religious reasons.

distinctions.note: Asexual describes a person who feels no sexual attraction, and it is often used as an identity; sexless describes a situation without sex.
Celibate describes a deliberate choice to avoid sex, often for religious or personal reasons; sexless does not imply choice.

examples.everyday: They've been married for twenty years, but she told me their marriage has been almost sexless since the kids were born.
examples.professional: The therapist said the couple had been sexless for almost two years, and she wanted to address that gently.
examples.analytical: Some theorists treat a sexless relationship as a sign of emotional distance rather than simply the absence of physical activity.

nuance.analogy: Like a house with the power off, the structure is there but nothing is running.
nuance.etymology: From sex, with the suffix -less, meaning without.
common_mistakes: Calling a single or celibate person sexless; that label is judgmental and usually inaccurate.
Confusing sexless with asexual, which describes a lack of sexual attraction rather than a lack of sexual activity.

senses.definition: Arising from the fact of being male or female; pertaining to sex or gender, or to the social relations between the sexes.
senses.example: Women face sexual discrimination in the workplace.

senses.definition: Pertaining to sexual intercourse or other intimate physical contact.
senses.example: Giving oral sex is my favorite sexual act.

senses.definition: Characterized by sexual feelings or behavior; possessing sexuality.
senses.example: She's a very sexual woman.

senses.definition: Pertaining to sexuality as a cultural phenomenon; relating to sexual behavior or conduct.
senses.example: a sexual innuendo

senses.definition: Capable of sexual reproduction; sexed, sexuate.
senses.example: Many fungi are sexual, combining genetic material from two parents during reproduction.

senses.definition: (rare) Experiencing sexual attraction; not asexual.
senses.example: The survey asked respondents whether they identified as asexual or sexual, with no other categories.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: A person who experiences sexual attraction, a person who has interest in or desire for sex.
senses.example: In the study, sexuals and asexuals reported very different dating preferences.

senses.definition: A species which reproduces by sexual rather than asexual reproduction, or a member of such a species.
senses.example: Unlike the asexual Daphnia clones, this species is a sexual that mates every season.

core.definition: Relating to sex, sexual activity, or sexual attraction.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The xu sound becomes sh, so the middle is shoo, and the last syllable is a weak uhl, not a full yoo-al.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in medical, legal and academic use; more charged or intimate in casual conversation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sexual as a neutral word in health, legal and school contexts, as in sexual health or sexual orientation. In casual conversation people often use sex or more informal words. Do not confuse sexual with sexy: sexual describes a fact or relationship, while sexy describes appeal.

distinctions.note: Sexy is informal and describes how attractive someone or something seems; sexual is neutral and describes what relates to sex.
Sexist means unfairly discriminatory on the basis of sex; sexual means related to sex or sexual activity.

examples.everyday: My doctor asked me some questions about my sexual health, which was a little awkward.
examples.professional: Our HR policy defines sexual harassment, and every manager must complete the training.
examples.analytical: Many philosophers argue that sexual desire involves more than biology, since it shapes meaning, identity and relationships.

nuance.analogy: If sex is a single note, sexual is the whole key that note belongs to.
nuance.etymology: From Latin sexualis, from sexus, sex.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle as yoo, as in SEKS-yoo-ul, instead of SEK-shoo-ul.
Using sexual to mean attractive; say sexy in that sense.

senses.definition: The cutting ability of an edge; keenness.
senses.example: The sharpness of the new chef's knife made slicing tomatoes effortless and clean.

senses.definition: The fineness of the point a pointed object.
senses.example: The sharpness of the needle made it easy to thread the suture through the fabric.

senses.definition: The product or result of being sharp.
senses.example: The sharpness of her criticism stung, though everyone agreed the report needed fixing.

senses.definition: Pungency or acidity.
senses.example: The sharpness of the green apples made my lips pucker after the first bite.

senses.definition: Distinctness, focus.
senses.example: The sharpness of the photograph revealed every leaf and wire on the distant fence.

senses.definition: Acuteness or acuity.
senses.example: Her sharpness at spotting statistical errors impressed the entire analytics team during the review.

core.definition: The quality of an edge or point that cuts easily; also quickness and precision of mind, senses or speech.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the r is pronounced, not dropped. Do not insert a vowel between the p and n; the word has only two syllables, with a syllabic n at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when describing knives, minds or precision; it turns negative when describing a harsh tone, as in 'sharpness in his voice'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sharpness for physical edges and for mental quickness, as in 'the sharpness of her memory'. For a critical or cutting tone of voice, say 'an edge to her voice' or 'sharpness in her tone', which can sound pointed. In photography and screens, Americans say 'image sharpness' or 'resolution' rather than 'clarity'.

distinctions.note: Keenness stresses eagerness or intense interest, while sharpness stresses cutting precision or quickness of perception.
Acuity is a more formal, technical word for sharpness of the senses, such as visual acuity, and is less common in everyday speech.

examples.everyday: This knife has lost its sharpness, so cutting tomatoes is a pain.
examples.professional: The lead designer asked the team to review the sharpness of the new interface's error messages before launch.
examples.analytical: Kant's sharpness in distinguishing theoretical from practical reason is what makes his argument so difficult to resist.

nuance.analogy: Sharpness is like a pencil point: a little wear and the line goes fuzzy.
nuance.etymology: From sharp (Old English scearp) plus the suffix -ness, meaning the quality of being sharp.
common_mistakes: Inserting an extra vowel, saying 'SHAR-puh-ness' instead of 'SHARP-nus'.
Using sharpness for a voice tone that is merely strict; 'sharpness' can sound harsh, so 'firmness' is often better.

sharpness.etymology: From Middle English *sharpnesse*, *scharpnesse*, from Old English *sċearpnes* (“sharpness”), equivalent to *sharp* + *-ness*.

senses.definition: The pastor of a church; one who guides others in religion.
senses.example: Our new shepherd preaches with patience and kindness to every family in the congregation.

senses.definition: A person who tends sheep, especially a grazing flock.
A male sheep tender.
senses.example: Before dawn, the shepherd led his flock across the frost-covered valley toward the spring pasture.

senses.definition: Someone who watches over, looks after, or guides somebody.
A male watcher/guardian/guider/leader.
senses.example: In the novel, the wise mentor becomes a shepherd to the orphaned boys.

senses.definition: A male pastor.
A German Shepherd.
senses.example: Our neighbor's German shepherd barks at every squirrel that crosses the backyard fence.

senses.definition: (poetic) A swain; a rustic male lover.
senses.example: In the old ballad, the shepherd sings beneath her window until the moon sets.
senses.label: poetic

senses.definition: To watch over; to guide.
senses.example: She shepherded the nervous first-year students through the crowded campus on orientation day.

core.definition: A person who looks after sheep, especially one who guides a flock to pasture and protects it; also a pastor who guides a congregation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SHEP. The final -herd is a single unstressed syllable with a reduced American r-colored vowel, so it sounds like 'erd', not 'hard'.

nuance.connotation: Positive, with warm, pastoral associations; the church sense is respectful.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use shepherd mainly for literal sheep farmers, in Bible passages, and in church language for a pastor. Calling a modern pastor a shepherd is common in Protestant churches. As a verb, 'to shepherd' means to guide people carefully through a process, which is common in meetings and projects.

distinctions.note: Pastor is the ordinary title of a church leader in American churches; shepherd is a more figurative, biblical image for the same role.
A herder can tend any livestock, while a shepherd specifically tends sheep.

collocations: tend the flock like a shepherd
shepherd the team through the release

examples.everyday: My uncle raises sheep in Montana, and he still works like a shepherd every morning.
examples.professional: I'll shepherd this proposal through the review board so the deadline holds.
examples.analytical: In the Psalms, the image of the shepherd presents God as one who provides, guides and protects his people.

nuance.analogy: A shepherd leads a flock the way a good project lead steers a team: watching closely and nudging people toward safe pasture.
nuance.etymology: From Old English sceaphierde, from sceap (sheep) and herde (herder, keeper).
common_mistakes: Spelling it 'shepard', which drops the e and changes the sound.
Pronouncing the last syllable as 'hard' rather than 'erd'.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew ro'eh (רֹעֶה), 'one who feeds or tends', and Greek poimen (ποιμήν), 'shepherd'. Psalm 23:1 declares that the Lord is the psalmist's shepherd, a picture of personal care. John 10:11 has Jesus call himself the good shepherd who gives his life for the sheep. Ezekiel 34:23 promises that God will set up one shepherd over his people, a David-like ruler, to feed them.

shepherd.etymology: From Middle English *schepherde*, from Old English *sċēaphierde*, a compound of *sċēap* (“sheep”) and *hierde* (“herdsman”), equivalent to modern *sheep* + *herd*.

senses.definition: The process of transporting goods from their point of origin to a customer, especially a consumer as end user; a charge supposed to cover the direct and indirect costs of doing so.
senses.example: The total came to forty dollars, plus eight dollars for shipping and handling.

core.definition: Charges added to an online or mail order to cover the costs of packing, handling, and sending the items to the buyer.

pronunciation.tip: Stress SHIP and HAN, with the first syllables strongest. Reduce 'and' to a weak uh-nd sound, and do not fully pronounce the -dl- of 'handling' as two separate vowels.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative. Shoppers often see it as an added cost they would rather not pay.
nuance.usage_note: Americans see this charge on online checkout pages, often abbreviated as S&H. Stores sometimes offer free shipping and handling as a promotion. In some contexts, Americans say postage and handling, or simply shipping, and the amount is usually listed separately from taxes.

distinctions.note: A delivery fee covers bringing an item to your door, often from a local store, while shipping and handling usually refers to sending a package by mail.
Sales tax is a government charge on the price, while shipping and handling is a fee set by the seller.

examples.everyday: The shirt was twenty dollars, but shipping and handling made the total thirty-two dollars.
examples.professional: Can you add shipping and handling to the purchase order before we approve the invoice?
examples.analytical: Economists treat shipping and handling as part of the total landed cost of goods, not as a separate convenience fee.

nuance.analogy: Shipping and handling is the toll on a bridge you did not build: you pay to cross from the store to your door.
nuance.etymology: Compound of shipping, from ship, and handling, from handle.
common_mistakes: Writing 'shipping & handling' in formal writing, where the full phrase is better.
Pronouncing 'handling' as 'HAN-dul-ing' with a separate vowel for the -dl- syllable, which sounds unnatural.

senses.definition: Surprised, startled, confused, or taken aback, particularly when also indignant.
senses.example: We were shocked to see how ill she was.

senses.definition: Subjected to electric shock.
senses.example: The technician was shocked when he touched the exposed wire in the panel.

senses.definition: Suffering from shock.
senses.example: The patient is shocked.

senses.definition: Affected, altered, or transformed by one or more shock waves.
senses.example: shocked quartz

core.definition: Very surprised or upset, often in a way that also feels offended or disapproving, by something unexpected or wrong.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the only syllable, and the vowel is the short open 'ah' of the cot-caught merger, not 'aw'. Pronounce the final 'ked' as a plain /t/, with no extra vowel after it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It signals surprise mixed with disapproval or distress, and it is strong, so use it for things that really upset you.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'I was shocked' or 'I'm shocked that...' for news or behavior that goes against your expectations, often ethical or social. Saying 'I'm so shocked!' is common in casual talk, but for mild surprise, 'surprised' or 'I didn't expect that' sounds more natural. Ironic use, such as 'Shocked, I tell you, shocked!', is a well-known joke.

distinctions.note: 'Surprised' is neutral and mild; 'shocked' is stronger and often carries moral or emotional distress.
'Stunned' suggests being speechless or dazed, while 'shocked' can also include anger or indignation.

examples.everyday: My neighbor was shocked when the package arrived with the wrong address.
examples.professional: We were shocked to see the error rate jump after the last deployment.
examples.analytical: Readers are rightly shocked by the author's indifference to the suffering he describes.

nuance.analogy: Like a sudden jolt from a live wire, the word signals a jolt to your expectations.
nuance.etymology: From 'shock,' from French 'choc,' meaning a clash or blow.
common_mistakes: Using 'shocked' for mild surprise, which can sound dramatic.
Saying 'I am shock' instead of 'I am shocked.'

conversation.text: I was shocked to hear they got divorced.
Everyone was shocked when the quiet guy won the talent show.
Don't look so shocked! I can cook, you know.

senses.definition: Showing clever resourcefulness in practical matters.
Artful, tricky or cunning.
Streetwise, street-smart.
Knowledgeable, intelligent, keen.
Nigh accurate.
senses.example: a shrewd guess

senses.definition: Severe, intense, hard.
senses.example: a shrewd blow, or assault

senses.definition: Sharp, snithy, piercing.
senses.example: a shrewd wind

core.definition: Good at judging situations and making practical decisions that benefit you, often with a sharp and calculating mind.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with the long OO sound of food. The r is pronounced in General American, and the sh sound is followed by a clear r, not a w or l sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive, meaning smart and capable, but it can shift to negative when it suggests cunning or manipulation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use shrewd in business news, politics and descriptions of people who make clever decisions. It is more formal than smart and is common in writing and speeches. In casual talk, people more often say 'smart' or 'street-smart.' Calling someone shrewd can imply they are willing to bend rules.

distinctions.note: Smart is the everyday word for intelligent, while shrewd specifically refers to practical judgment and calculated decision-making.
Clever can suggest cleverness in a playful or ingenious way, while shrewd suggests careful judgment for gain.

examples.everyday: That was a shrewd move to buy the tickets early.
examples.professional: It was a shrewd decision to delay the product launch until we had better test data.
examples.analytical: The shrewd agent weighs incentives carefully, which distinguishes practical judgment from mere intelligence.

nuance.analogy: Like a chess player who sees three moves ahead.
nuance.etymology: From shrew, referring to a sharp or cunning person, with an older sense of wicked or malicious.
common_mistakes: Using shrewd to mean simply intelligent without the sense of practical calculation.
Pronouncing the vowel as the short oo sound of book.

shrewd.etymology: From Middle English *schrewed* (“depraved; wicked”), from *schrewen* (“to curse; beshrew”), from *schrewe*, *schrowe*, *screwe* (“evil or wicked person/thing”), from Old English *sċrēawa* (“wicked person”).

senses.definition: Easily frightened; timid.
senses.example: My shy daughter hid behind her mother whenever a stranger spoke to her at church.

senses.definition: Reserved; disinclined to familiar approach.
senses.example: He is very shy with strangers.

senses.definition: Cautious; wary; suspicious.
senses.example: Although the new coworker seemed friendly, I was shy about trusting his motives at first.

senses.definition: Short, insufficient or less than.
senses.example: By our count your shipment came up two shy of the bill of lading amount.

senses.definition: Less likely to reveal whom they will vote for than average, chiefly in the context of the collective effect this has on polling accuracy.
senses.example: Pollsters need to remember the shy Tory factor.

senses.definition: To avoid due to caution, embarrassment or timidness.
senses.example: She shied away from the spotlight and never volunteered to speak at team meetings.

senses.definition: To jump back in fear.
senses.example: The horse shied at the unexpected approach of a motor vehicle.

senses.definition: To throw sideways with a jerk; to fling.
senses.example: to shy a stone

senses.definition: An act of throwing.
senses.example: The fielder's wild shy at the stumps sailed over the wicketkeeper's head for four runs.

senses.definition: A place for throwing.
senses.example: coconut shy

senses.definition: A sudden start aside, as by a horse.
senses.example: The horse gave a sudden shy at the plastic bag blowing across the trail, nearly unseating me.

senses.definition: In the Eton College wall game, a point scored by lifting the ball against the wall in the calx.
senses.example: In the wall game at Eton, a shy scored when the ball struck the wall within the calx.

core.definition: Nervous or uncomfortable around other people, especially new people, and reluctant to speak or be noticed.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a long i like 'eye.' Don't add a y sound after the sh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use shy for people who are quiet or reserved in social situations, and it is generally neutral or gently positive when describing children or adults. Calling an adult shy can sound mildly condescending, so you might say 'reserved' or 'quiet' in professional settings. In a professional context, 'I'm a little shy' is a natural self-description.

distinctions.note: Timid suggests fear or lack of courage, which is stronger than shy.
Bashful is old-fashioned and often used for children or light embarrassment.
Reserved describes someone who keeps their feelings private, which may be a choice rather than nervousness.

examples.everyday: My new neighbor is a little shy, but she waves every morning.
examples.professional: Some people on the team are shy in big meetings, so I usually ask them for written comments first.
examples.analytical: Shyness is often understood as a combination of social anxiety and a desire to avoid negative judgment, not simply a lack of interest in others.

nuance.analogy: Think of shyness as a turtle that pulls its head in when a stranger approaches, then comes out once it feels safe.
common_mistakes: Saying 'shy of' when you mean 'shy about' or 'shy to' (use 'shy of' for avoiding something, and 'shy about' for embarrassment).
Using 'shy' for someone who is simply quiet and not uncomfortable; shy implies some nervousness.

shy.etymology: From Middle English *shy* (“shy”), from Old English *sċēoh* (“shy”), from **skeuh* (“shy, fearful”), from Proto-Germanic **skeuhaz* (“shy, fearful”).

conversation.text: My daughter is really shy around new people.
Don't be shy. Help yourself to some food.
He was too shy to ask her to dance.
She's a little shy at first, but she opens up once she knows you.
Don't be shy! Come say hi.
My son is too shy to order his own food.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to unmarried people.
senses.example: a singles bar

senses.definition: Synonym of tubulars.
senses.example: The racer glued fresh singles onto her carbon wheels before the criterium began.

senses.definition: A game between individual players.
senses.example: The final singles match lasted three hours before the champion finally won the set.

core.definition: Unmarried people, especially those without a partner and often looking to date.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The final 'gles' is a syllabic l, so it sounds like 'SING-gulz,' not 'sin-gulls.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can sound light or playful in dating contexts, and it is not usually considered rude.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'singles' as a plural noun for unmarried adults, especially in phrases like 'singles night' at a bar or church group. Saying 'a single' for one unmarried person is less common in speech. In tennis and other sports, 'singles' means a match between two individual players, as opposed to 'doubles.'

distinctions.note: 'Single' is the adjective for one person who is not married, while 'singles' is the plural noun for a group of such people.
Unattached is more formal and describes a person who is not in a romantic relationship, but it is rarely used for social groups.

examples.everyday: The church has a singles group that meets on Friday nights for dinner.
examples.professional: Our HR survey shows that singles are more willing to accept relocation offers than employees with children.
examples.analytical: Demographers track the rising share of singles in urban areas as one factor behind declining birth rates.

nuance.analogy: 'Singles' is like a waiting room of unmatched people: each one is available, and the group is defined by that shared status.
nuance.etymology: From 'single,' from Latin singulus ('one at a time').
common_mistakes: Using 'singles' to mean one person; for one person, say 'a single.'
Pronouncing the ending as 'sin-gulls' rather than 'SING-gulz.'

senses.definition: In a sinuous manner.

core.definition: In a winding, curving, or gracefully twisting way, often describing smooth, snake-like movement.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable. The -ous ending is a reduced us, not oos, and the -ly is a light, unstressed ending.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests elegance, grace, or flowing motion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sinuously mainly for graceful movement, such as a dancer or a snake, or for a road or river that curves gently. It is more literary than winding and sounds elegant. In casual talk people usually say winds or curves instead.

distinctions.note: Gracefully focuses only on elegance, while sinuously adds the sense of curving or snake-like movement.
Winding is common and neutral, while sinuously is more literary and suggests grace or sensuality.
Meandering suggests aimless wandering, while sinuously suggests controlled, flowing curves.

examples.everyday: The trail winds sinuously up the hill, so the hike takes a while longer than you expect.
examples.professional: The new bike lane runs sinuously between the buildings, which makes it hard to see cars coming from the street.
examples.analytical: The prose moves sinuously between memory and argument, so that each claim seems to loop back on the one before.

nuance.analogy: Like a snake sliding across warm sand, it moves in smooth, repeated bends rather than in straight lines.
nuance.etymology: From sinuous, from Latin sinuosus, full of curves, with the adverbial ending -ly.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, as in sin-YOO-us-lee; the stress belongs on SIN.
Using sinuously for ordinary turning in plain speech, where winding is more natural.

senses.definition: To rest in a state of reduced consciousness.
senses.example: You should sleep eight hours a day.

senses.definition: To have sexual intercourse (see sleep with).
senses.example: Last night we slept together for the first time.

senses.definition: To accommodate in beds.
senses.example: This caravan can sleep four people comfortably.

senses.definition: To be careless, inattentive, or unconcerned; not to be vigilant; to live thoughtlessly.
senses.example: We cannot sleep on security now, because hackers never take a day off.

senses.definition: To be dead.
senses.example: They say the old king now sleeps beneath the cathedral floor.

senses.definition: To be, or appear to be, in repose; to be quiet; to be unemployed, unused, or unagitated; to rest; to lie dormant.
senses.example: a question sleeps for the present; the law sleeps

senses.definition: To wait for a period of time without performing any action.
senses.example: After a failed connection attempt, the program sleeps for 5 seconds before trying again.

senses.definition: To place into a state of hibernation.
senses.example: The lab team could sleep the mice for weeks to study metabolism.

senses.definition: To spin on its axis with no other perceptible motion.
senses.example: When a top is sleeping, it is spinning without precessing.

senses.definition: To cause (a spinning top or yo-yo) to spin on its axis with no other perceptible motion.
senses.example: Watch how he can sleep a yo-yo for a full minute without any wobble.

senses.definition: To knock (someone) out (as, in a fight).
senses.example: The boxer's right hook could sleep an opponent in a single punch.

senses.definition: The state of reduced consciousness during which a human or animal rests in a daily rhythm.
senses.example: I really need some sleep.

senses.definition: An act or instance of sleeping.
senses.example: I’m just going to have a quick sleep.

senses.definition: A night.
senses.example: There are only three sleeps till Christmas!

senses.definition: Rheum, crusty or gummy discharge found in the corner of the eyes after waking, whether real or a figurative objectification of sleep (in the sense of reduced consciousness).
senses.example: Mom wiped the sleep from my eyes before breakfast.

senses.definition: The hibernation of animals.
senses.example: The bear's winter sleep lasted nearly five months in the mountain den.

senses.definition: A state of plants, usually at night, when their leaflets approach each other and the flowers close and droop, or are covered by the folded leaves.
senses.example: Clover leaves fold down during sleep, closing up the flowers each night.

core.definition: To rest in a state of reduced consciousness, with your eyes closed and your body inactive, usually at night.

pronunciation.tip: Use the long ee vowel, as in see, and do not shorten it to the short i of slip. Americans usually make the final p clearly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. Sleep is a basic everyday word. It turns negative only through related words such as sleepless or sleep-deprived, which describe the lack of it.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say I'm going to bed or I'm going to sleep, and both sound natural. Go to sleep is a common instruction to children, and Sleep tight is a warm goodnight. Sleep in means to sleep later than usual in the morning, and sleep on it means to think about a decision overnight, both of which you will hear often.

distinctions.note: To doze is to sleep lightly for a short time, often without meaning to; sleep covers any length of rest.
Rest means relaxing or not working and does not necessarily involve sleep.
A nap is a short sleep during the day; sleep is the general word and can mean a full night of rest.

examples.everyday: I'm exhausted, so I'm going to bed early and try to get some sleep.
examples.professional: Please don't schedule the release review for tomorrow morning; the team has had almost no sleep this week.
examples.analytical: Aristotle wrote a short treatise on sleep and waking, asking what sleep is and how it differs from death.

nuance.analogy: Sleep works like a nightly reset: the mind rests while the body repairs itself, much as a computer restarts to clear its memory.
nuance.etymology: From Old English slǣpan, to sleep; related to German schlafen.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like slip with a short i, which is a different word in English.
Treating sleep as countable, as in a sleep, for ordinary rest; the natural phrase is get some sleep, since sleep is usually uncountable.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture sleep is both literal rest and a figure for death. The Greek words are hypnos, sleep, and koimaō, to fall asleep, which the New Testament uses of death. Key passages: John 11:11-14, where Jesus says Lazarus has fallen asleep and then makes plain that he has died; 1 Thessalonians 4:13-14, where Paul speaks of those who have fallen asleep in Jesus; and Psalm 121:4, which says that the Keeper of Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps.

sleep.etymology: From Middle English *slepen*, from *slēpan*, from **slāpan*, from Proto-Germanic **slēpaną* (“to sleep”).

senses.definition: A stationary, often triangular object that launches any ball that hits its longest side back at a high force, now usually located above the flipper and between it and the inlane, with one each for both lower flippers.
senses.example: The ball struck the slingshot and shot back up, earning the player bonus points.

senses.definition: A sling bikini.
senses.example: She wore a bright yellow slingshot to the pool party.

senses.definition: An implement of a broad fabric worn around and connecting both bicipites brachii to support benching the most heavy weights.
senses.example: He strapped on a slingshot before attempting his heaviest bench press.

senses.definition: Synonym of slingshot effect.
senses.example: The probe used a slingshot around Jupiter to reach the outer planets faster.

senses.definition: To move or cause to move in a manner resembling a projectile shot from a slingshot.
senses.example: The car slingshot forward as soon as the light turned green.

senses.definition: To use the gravity of a moving planet to add momentum to a spacecraft.
senses.example: The shuttle will slingshot around Jupiter on its way to Saturn.

senses.definition: To perform the slingshot maneuver (see Noun).
senses.example: The racer slingshot around the lead car to take first place.

core.definition: A Y-shaped stick with an elastic band attached to a pouch, used to shoot small stones or pellets by pulling and releasing it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SLING, with a lighter secondary stress on the second word. The second syllable has the open 'ah' vowel of cot, so say 'shot' with that vowel, not 'shoot'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly playful; it can imply childish mischief or, in a safety context, a dangerous object.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use slingshot for the Y-shaped toy that children use to shoot pebbles or rubber bands. British speakers normally say catapult for this object, so use catapult if you are in London or reading British sources. In American English, slingshot can also be a verb meaning to move rapidly, as in slingshot around a planet, which appears in physics and space news.

distinctions.note: A sling is a loop of cloth or straps used to throw a stone or to support an injured arm; a slingshot is a Y-shaped stick with elastic.
Catapult is the general British term and also refers to large historical war machines; in American English slingshot is the everyday toy word.

examples.everyday: My little brother got in trouble for shooting pigeons with a slingshot in the backyard.
examples.professional: The safety manager banned slingshots from the warehouse after a near-miss with a steel bolt.
examples.analytical: A slingshot stores elastic energy and converts it into a fast projectile, so its physics shows how tension can be turned into motion.

nuance.analogy: A slingshot is like a bow and arrow shrunk into one hand, where the elastic does the drawing for you.
nuance.etymology: From sling (a loop or strap for throwing) plus shot, the thing thrown.
common_mistakes: Using catapult in American conversation for a toy; Americans will understand, but slingshot is the natural word.
Pronouncing the second syllable with the 'oo' of shoot; it has the short cot vowel.

senses.definition: To slow; to slow down; to decelerate.

core.definition: To slow down; to reduce speed or pace, often because you or someone else needs time.

pronunciation.tip: In this phrasal verb the stress falls on 'up', with secondary stress on 'slow', so say 'sloh-UP' with 'up' clearly emphasized. Keep the 'u' in 'up' short and relaxed.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly informal. It can sound friendly when asking someone to wait, and neutral when describing a process.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech, 'slow down' is far more common than 'slow up', so 'slow up' sounds slightly less standard. You will hear it mostly in casual requests, such as 'Slow up a little, I can't keep up!' A natural reply is 'Sorry, I'll slow down.'

distinctions.note: Slow down is the standard, far more common phrasal verb in everyday American speech, while slow up is more informal.
Decelerate is a technical or formal term for reducing speed, used in physics and engineering rather than casual conversation.

collocations: slow up when you get there

examples.everyday: Slow up a little, Mike, I can't keep up with you!
examples.professional: Let's slow up the rollout until the monitoring dashboards show stable error rates.
examples.analytical: The argument slowed up at its crucial premise, so each step now needs independent justification.

nuance.analogy: Like easing off the gas pedal on a hill, so the car settles into a calmer speed.
common_mistakes: Using 'slow up' in formal writing where 'slow down' or 'decelerate' is more standard.
Placing a pronoun after 'slow' incorrectly, as in 'slow up it', rather than 'slow it up'.

senses.definition: A smoke detector.

core.definition: A device on a ceiling or wall that makes a loud sound to warn people when it detects smoke, usually from a fire.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second word, ALARM, with a lighter stress on SMOKE. The unstressed syllable of alarm is a reduced schwa, so say uh-LAHRM, not ah-LARM, and pronounce the r clearly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It refers to a safety device, so the word itself carries no emotional charge, though it signals an emergency when it sounds.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say smoke alarm or smoke detector for this device, and both are common in homes, apartments and building codes. People say the alarm is going off when it beeps or shrieks, and a common request is to change the battery or test the alarm. Calling it a smoke detector is slightly more technical and is common in official or inspection contexts.

distinctions.note: Nearly identical in meaning; smoke detector is more technical and used by fire departments and building inspectors, while smoke alarm is the everyday household term.
A fire alarm is usually a building-wide system, often pulled manually, while a smoke alarm is a single device that senses smoke on its own.

examples.everyday: The smoke alarm keeps going off whenever I make toast, so I need to move it.
examples.professional: Facilities confirmed that every unit on the third floor has a working smoke alarm before the inspection.
examples.analytical: A smoke alarm reduces risk by converting an invisible hazard into an audible signal, but it cannot prevent the fire itself.

nuance.analogy: A smoke alarm is like a watchdog that barks at the first whiff of trouble, long before you can see the flames.
nuance.etymology: Smoke comes from Old English smoca; alarm comes from Italian all'arme, meaning 'to arms'.
common_mistakes: Saying smoke alarm with the stress on the wrong word, as in SMOKE alarm instead of smoke ah-LARM.
Pronouncing alarm as ah-LARM with a clear, long vowel instead of the reduced uh-LAHRM.

senses.definition: The act of swimming using a snorkel.

core.definition: The activity of swimming on or near the water surface while breathing through a snorkel and looking at the underwater scene.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle vowel is a quick schwa, and the final -ing is a clear, short "ing".

nuance.connotation: Neutral and positive. It usually describes a relaxing vacation or outdoor activity.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use "snorkeling" as a noun for the hobby or activity, usually on vacation in places with clear water, such as Hawaii, Florida, or the Caribbean. You can say "We went snorkeling" or "Snorkeling was amazing." People often compare it to scuba diving, which is a deeper and more equipment-heavy activity. Reply with enthusiasm, for example, "Oh, did you see any turtles?"

distinctions.note: Scuba diving uses tanks and goes deeper; snorkeling stays at the surface.
Swimming is general movement in water; snorkeling specifically means swimming with a breathing tube to watch underwater.

examples.everyday: Snorkeling was the best part of our trip to Maui; we saw sea turtles right off the beach.
examples.professional: For the offsite, we booked a snorkeling tour, so everyone should send their shoe size for fins by Friday.
examples.analytical: Snorkeling reveals a world that is visible but not fully accessible, a kind of partial intimacy with nature.

nuance.analogy: Snorkeling is like looking through a window in the water: you float on the surface and see a whole world below you.
nuance.etymology: Formed from snorkel with the English -ing suffix, making a noun for the activity.
common_mistakes: Saying "I do snorkeling" in casual speech; Americans more often say "I go snorkeling."
Pronouncing the word as "snork-ell-ing" with the middle syllable stressed.

conversation.text: We went snorkeling in Hawaii and saw so many fish.
Is the water clear enough for snorkeling today?
Snorkeling is easy; you just float and breathe through the tube.

senses.definition: Of or relating to socialism.
Having socialist tendencies.

core.definition: Having features or tendencies associated with socialism, such as government control of key industries or large public programs, often used to criticize a policy.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on the third syllable, -LIS-, and the -tic ending is pronounced tik. Many learners put the stress too early or pronounce the -ic as a long ee sound.

nuance.connotation: Often negative in American political talk. It suggests that something goes too far toward government control, though a supporter might use it neutrally.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use socialistic mostly in criticism, as in 'a socialistic healthcare plan,' to suggest that policies resemble socialism. It is less exact than socialist and is less common in formal writing. For a neutral description of a political movement, say socialist. In conversation it sounds opinionated, so use it knowing that others may hear it as a judgment.

distinctions.note: Socialist refers directly to people, parties, or ideas that support socialism, while socialistic describes something that resembles socialism, often in a critical way.
Collectivist emphasizes group interests over individual ones in general, while socialistic specifically refers to economic systems with public ownership or control.

examples.everyday: My dad thinks the new parking plan is too socialistic, but my roommate says the city just needs more buses.
examples.professional: The finance team warned that the proposed rent-control policy could be seen as socialistic by investors.
examples.analytical: Critics describe the reform as socialistic, but its defenders argue that public provision of basic services does not necessarily mean collective ownership of production.

nuance.analogy: Like a restaurant that slowly takes over every menu decision: each step may seem small, but together they change the whole character of the place.
nuance.etymology: From socialist plus -ic, meaning having the nature of or resembling.
common_mistakes: Using socialistic as a neutral synonym for socialist, when it often sounds like criticism.
Stressing the first syllable, as in SOH-shuh-listic, instead of the third syllable.

core.definition: A town in the lowlands of Judah, in the Shephelah, that appears in Joshua, Samuel and Chronicles, and is the place where the Philistines gathered before David fought Goliath.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SOH, and pronounce the final syllable as 'oh', not 'uh'. The 'k' is a clear sound in both syllables.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a historical place name used in biblical study.
nuance.usage_note: Americans encounter Socoh in Bible study, reading the Old Testament and in discussions of biblical geography. It is not used in everyday conversation. In a church or Bible study setting, someone might say 'Socoh was a town near the Valley of Elah', which is a natural way to place it.

distinctions.note: Azekah was a neighboring town near Socoh; both guarded the approach to the Valley of Elah and are mentioned together in 1 Samuel 17:1.
Socoh and Sochoh are spellings of the same name in different Bible translations, so the spelling depends on the version used.

examples.everyday: Our Bible study group looked at a map and found Socoh in the lowlands west of Jerusalem.
examples.professional: In the lesson on the Israelite kingdom, we placed Socoh among the fortified towns of the Shephelah.
examples.analytical: The Philistine gathering at Socoh, set against the Israelite camp in the Valley of Elah, frames David's victory over Goliath within a contest over strategic territory.

nuance.analogy: Socoh is like a guard post on a hillside road, placed to watch the approach to a valley that armies had to cross.
nuance.etymology: From the Hebrew name Sokho, whose meaning is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the name as 'SOH-kuh' rather than 'SOH-koh'.
Confusing Socoh with Sodom or Socrates, which are unrelated names.
nuance.biblical_note: Socoh was a town in the Shephelah, the foothill region between the Judean hill country and the coastal plain. Joshua 15:35 lists Socoh among the towns of Judah in that lowland region. 1 Samuel 17:1 says the Philistines gathered at Socoh before the battle in which David defeated Goliath. 2 Chronicles 11:7 records that Rehoboam fortified Socoh among his defensive cities.

senses.definition: One's male offspring.
senses.example: Before the birth of the man's child, he said: "I want a son, not a daughter."

senses.definition: A male adopted person in relation to his adoptive parents.
A male person who has such a close relationship with an older or otherwise more authoritative person that he can be regarded as a son of the other person.
senses.example: Marcus has always been like a son to our neighbor, who taught him to fish.

senses.definition: A male person considered to have been significantly shaped by social conflict.
senses.example: He was a son of the mafia system.

senses.definition: A person regarded as the product of some place.
senses.example: She was a son of Brooklyn, and she never let anyone forget it.

senses.definition: A familiar address to a male person from an older or otherwise more authoritative person.
senses.example: Put down that cookie, son, and tell me where you found the money.

senses.definition: An informal address to a friend or person of equal authority.
senses.example: Hey, son, you still owe me twenty bucks from last weekend's game.

senses.definition: The current version of a file, derived from the preceding father file.
senses.example: Before we merge, check that the latest son of the report file includes my edits.

senses.definition: Son cubano, a genre of music and dance blending Spanish and African elements that originated in Cuba during the late 19th century.
senses.example: The band played a lively son cubano that had the whole dance floor moving.

senses.definition: To produce (i.e. bear, father, beget) a son.
senses.example: After three daughters, the couple hoped the next child would son them.

senses.definition: To address (someone) as "son".
senses.example: The old fisherman sons every young deckhand who comes aboard his boat.

core.definition: A male child in relation to his parents; one's male offspring.

pronunciation.tip: Say it as one short syllable that rhymes with fun and done. It is a homophone of sun in General American, so context carries the meaning.

nuance.connotation: Warm and neutral. As a form of address, 'son' can be affectionate, friendly, or firm depending on tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use son constantly in family talk, and older people often address younger men as son in a warm, slightly paternal way ('Watch your step, son'). Used this way it can sound patronizing if the speaker is not much older. The verb sense, to address someone as son, is informal, and in the phrase 'son of a gun' it is a mild exclamation.

distinctions.note: Child is gender-neutral and can refer to any offspring; son specifically means a male child.
Boy refers to a male of young age regardless of family; son emphasizes the parent-child relationship.
A stepson is the child of one's spouse from a previous relationship, while a son is a child of one's own or an adoptive relationship.

examples.everyday: Our son just started college in Ohio, and we're still getting used to the empty house.
examples.professional: I'm out Friday because my son has a dental appointment, but I'll be on email if anything urgent comes up.
examples.analytical: In the Gospel of John, Jesus describes the Son as one who does only what he sees the Father do.

nuance.analogy: Like a family name that passes from one generation to the next, carrying a line of relationship forward.
nuance.etymology: From Old English sunu, from Proto-Germanic *sunuz.
common_mistakes: Confusing son with sun, which is a homophone in American speech and easy to mix up in writing.
Pronouncing it with a long o, as in 'soan', instead of a short vowel.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture the key Hebrew word is ben (son, child, descendant), and the key Greek word is huios (son). Psalm 2:7 in the RSV describes the king as God's son, and Mark 1:11 records the voice at Jesus' baptism declaring him God's beloved Son. Romans 8:14 says those led by the Spirit of God are sons of God, extending the sonship language to believers.

son.etymology: From Middle English *sonn*, *sone*, *sun*, *sune*, from Old English *sunu* (“son”), from **sunu*, from Proto-Germanic **sunuz* (“son”), from Proto-Indo-European **suHnús* (“son”), from Proto-Indo-European **sewH-* (“to bear; give birth”).

senses.definition: A female animal, particularly: A female pig.
senses.example: The farmer's sow gave birth to twelve piglets in the barn last night.

senses.definition: A female pig.
senses.example: Our prize sow won the county fair's blue ribbon for the largest litter.

senses.definition: A female bear; she-bear.
senses.example: The hikers kept their distance from the sow and her cubs near the creek.

senses.definition: A female guinea pig.
senses.example: The veterinarian said the sow was pregnant, so we moved her to a separate cage.

senses.definition: A contemptible, often fat woman.
senses.example: Don't listen to that old sow; she's just spreading gossip again.

senses.definition: Clipping of sowbug.
senses.example: We found a dozen sows hiding under the damp log in the garden.

senses.definition: A channel that conducts molten metal to molds.
senses.example: The foundry worker poured molten iron down the sow into the waiting molds.

senses.definition: A mass of metal solidified in a mold.
senses.example: After the furnace cooled, we pulled a heavy iron sow from the sand mold.

senses.definition: A kind of covered shed, formerly used by besiegers in filling up and passing the ditch of a besieged place, sapping and mining the wall, etc.
senses.example: The engineers pushed a sow up against the castle wall to undermine its foundations.

senses.definition: To scatter, disperse, or plant (seeds).
senses.example: When I had sown the field, the day's work was over.

senses.definition: To spread abroad; to propagate.
senses.example: as you sow, so shall you reap

senses.definition: To scatter over; to besprinkle.

core.definition: To scatter or plant seeds in the ground so they will grow.

pronunciation.tip: The verb to sow rhymes with 'go', with the long o vowel. The pig sense, pronounced /saʊ/ like 'cow', is a different word with the same spelling.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'sow seeds' for planting in a garden or field, most often in farming, gardening or literary speech. In everyday talk, people more often say 'plant'. Figurative uses, like 'sow discord', are common in news and writing.

distinctions.note: Plant is the everyday word for putting seeds or plants into the ground; sow emphasizes scattering seeds and is more formal or literary.
Seed can be a verb meaning to put seed into soil, but it is less common for broad scattering.

examples.everyday: We're going to sow some beans in the back yard this weekend.
examples.professional: The marketing team wants to sow awareness of the new feature before the launch.
examples.analytical: Paul writes that whatever a person sows, that will he also reap, linking conduct to consequence.

nuance.analogy: Like scattering handfuls of seeds across a field, letting the soil take them in.
nuance.etymology: From Old English sawan (to scatter seed), related to Latin serere (to sow).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing sow as /saʊ/ when you mean to plant seeds; that sounds like the pig sense.
Using 'sow' in the past tense as 'sowed' in all cases; 'sown' is also common in the participle.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word behind sow is zara (Hebrew זָרַע), meaning to sow seed; the Greek word is speirō, meaning to sow. Matthew 13:3 introduces the parable of the sower, who scatters seed on different kinds of ground. Galatians 6:7-8 says that a person reaps what he sows. 2 Corinthians 9:6 says that whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly.

senses.definition: An unwanted call, usually automated advertising.

core.definition: An unwanted phone call, usually automated, that tries to sell something or scam you.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SPAM, and the two words are linked smoothly. The vowel in call is the same as in caught for most Americans, so it sounds like 'KAWL'.

nuance.connotation: Negative
nuance.usage_note: Americans use spam call in everyday talk about phone annoyances, such as 'I got another spam call about my car warranty.' A natural reply is 'Just ignore it' or 'Don't pick up unknown numbers.' Say it casually with friends; in business, people usually say 'robocall' or 'unsolicited call.'

distinctions.note: A robocall is any automated call, including legitimate ones; a spam call is an unwanted call, often a scam.
Telemarketing calls are sales calls by people, and may be legal; spam calls are often automated and deceptive.

examples.everyday: Ugh, I just got another spam call about my car's extended warranty.
examples.professional: Our support line got flooded with spam calls, so we turned on call screening for unknown numbers.
examples.analytical: The rise of spam calls shows how cheap automated dialing shifts costs onto ordinary people.

nuance.analogy: Like junk mail that rings your doorbell instead of landing in your mailbox.
nuance.etymology: Spam (from the 1930s canned meat, later used for unwanted messages) and call (from Old English ceallian).
