distinctions.note: A laggard is something or someone that falls behind others; it is more literary and can sound harsher than underperformer.
An underachiever is a person whose ability exceeds their results, usually in school or work; underperformer applies more broadly to companies and funds.

examples.everyday: My old car is the underperformer in our driveway; it never starts in winter.
examples.professional: We'll sell the two underperformers and move that budget to the new product line.
examples.analytical: Calling a company an underperformer tells us only its results relative to a benchmark, not whether its management is competent.

nuance.analogy: Like the bench player whose numbers keep falling below the rest of the lineup.
nuance.etymology: From underperform plus the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Using underperformer for a process or plan; it describes a person or thing that performs poorly.
Stressing the wrong syllable; the main stress is on FOR, not PER.

senses.definition: Not able to be proven false, but not necessarily true.
senses.example: Conspiracy theories are designed to be unfalsifiable: every criticism can be dismissed as "whitewashing by the conspirers", and every concern can be summarized as "part of the greater conspiracy".

senses.definition: A statement or argument that cannot be proven false, but is not necessarily true.
senses.example: A model that explains every outcome is unfalsifiable and therefore useless for testing hypotheses.

core.definition: Structured so that no possible observation or test could prove it false; a claim that cannot be refuted, which does not make it true.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the -fai- syllable, not on fal-, and the -able ending reduces to a quick uh-bul. Many learners put stress on the first syllable of falsify, but in unfalsifiable the stress moves to the fai syllable.

nuance.connotation: Usually negative when used to criticize a theory or claim, because it suggests the idea escapes all testing. In philosophy of science it is a neutral technical term describing a logical property.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in philosophy, science, and debate, often to criticize a theory that explains every outcome. You will hear it in discussions of Karl Popper's criterion, of conspiracy theories, or of arguments that cannot lose. It is not used in casual conversation about everyday facts.

distinctions.note: Unverifiable means no evidence can confirm the claim; unfalsifiable means no evidence can refute it. A claim can be both, or one without the other.
Unprovable refers to lacking a proof, which is a question of confirmation; unfalsifiable is about a claim's immunity to disproof.

examples.everyday: My uncle says the stock market always follows his gut, but whenever he is wrong he just says he was misread, which makes his argument unfalsifiable.
examples.professional: The vendor's model explains every outage as a planned test, so our monitoring team pointed out that the claim is unfalsifiable and cannot be checked against the logs.
examples.analytical: A theory that absorbs every counterexample by adding auxiliary assumptions risks becoming unfalsifiable, and Popper argued that such theories lie outside empirical science.

nuance.analogy: An unfalsifiable claim is like a referee who calls every play in your favor no matter what happened on the field, so the game can never be lost.
nuance.etymology: From un- (not) plus falsifiable, from Latin falsus (false) and facere (to make).
common_mistakes: Thinking unfalsifiable means false; it means no possible test could show it false, which says nothing about whether it is true.
Stressing the first syllable, as in FAL-si-fy-uh-bul, instead of the -fai- syllable.

senses.definition: False, not genuine or authentic.

core.definition: Not real or authentic; false, fake, or insincere, especially in feelings, apologies, or expressions of interest.

pronunciation.tip: Stress JEN, the first syllable of the root. Say the ending as in in, not eye-n, and many Americans make the middle sound like yoo-wun.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests that someone's feeling or statement is not sincere, though it is milder than calling it a lie.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use ungenuine in casual speech; they say fake, insincere, or not real. It is more common in writing and formal criticism, such as a review of a performance or an analysis of an apology. Because it is less common, a listener may pause, so in conversation prefer insincere or fake.

distinctions.note: Fake means deliberately made to deceive, while ungenuine can describe a feeling or expression that lacks authenticity without a clear plan to deceive.
Insincere refers to a person who says things they do not really mean, while ungenuine can describe objects, art, or emotions as well.
Counterfeit means a copy made to pass as the real thing, such as fake money, while ungenuine is a looser word for lacking authenticity.

examples.professional: The vendor's apology sounded ungenuine, so we asked for a written commitment with a clear timeline.
examples.analytical: A confession made only to escape punishment is ungenuine, since it expresses fear of consequences rather than a changed will.

nuance.analogy: Like a painted apple: it looks ripe from a distance, but there is no fruit inside.
nuance.etymology: From un- plus genuine, from Latin genuinus, natural, native, or true.
common_mistakes: Saying un-JEN-you-wine with the ending as eye-n; the ending is in or -yoo-in in careful speech.
Using ungenuine in casual conversation where Americans would say fake or insincere.
Confusing genuine with gentle or general; the stress and vowels differ.
nuance.biblical_note: The RSV does not use the word ungenuine, but the idea appears as love without hypocrisy. Romans 12:9 says, Let love be genuine, and the Greek is anypokritos, meaning without pretense or hypocrisy. In 2 Corinthians 6:6 Paul lists genuine love among the marks of his ministry, using the same Greek word. These passages suggest that the opposite of an ungenuine act is love that is not feigned.

senses.definition: Any cream containing medicinal ingredients applied to the skin for therapeutic purposes.
senses.example: The nurse rubbed a soothing unguent into the burn on his hand.

senses.definition: Taking the form of a cream or ointment.
senses.example: The herbal remedy came in an unguent form that she spread gently over her cracked knuckles.

core.definition: A cream or ointment applied to the skin for healing, soothing or protection.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, UNG. In American speech the gu is pronounced like gw, so say 'ung-wunt', not 'ung-yoo-ent'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a substance, though its old-fashioned tone can make it sound poetic or antiquated.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use unguent in everyday speech. It appears in medical history, literary writing and some pharmacy or cosmetic contexts. For a modern product, people say cream, ointment, salve or balm, and unguent can sound old-fashioned in ordinary conversation.

distinctions.note: Ointment is the common modern word for a medicated cream, while unguent is more literary and archaic.
Balm often suggests a soothing or fragrant substance, while unguent is a general term for any medicinal cream.

examples.professional: The wound-care protocol specifies a medicated ointment rather than a liquid, though the older documents still call it an unguent.
examples.analytical: The ancient recipe describes an unguent of resin and oil prepared for ritual anointing rather than simply for healing the skin.

nuance.analogy: Like an old apothecary jar on a shelf, a word that belongs to the past more than to the pharmacy today.
nuance.etymology: From Latin unguentum, 'ointment', from ungere, 'to anoint'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'un-gyoo-ent' as a rule; the American common pronunciation is 'UNG-wunt'.
Using unguent in everyday talk where ointment or cream would be natural.

unguent.etymology: Latin *unguentum* (“ointment”), from *unguō* (“to smear with ointment”), from Proto-Indo-European **h₃engʷ-* (“to salve, anoint”).

senses.definition: An institution of higher education that provides facilities for teaching, research, and the conferral of academic degrees across undergraduate, graduate, and often professional levels.
senses.example: She's studying mathematics at university.

core.definition: A school of higher education that offers undergraduate and graduate degrees and does research.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on VUR, the same syllable as in 'universe' but with a different ending. The final -ty is a reduced 'tee' sound, and the word is often shortened to 'uni' in British speech, which Americans rarely use.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; prestige depends on the particular school, and the word signals a large institution with graduate programs.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'university' for large institutions that include graduate schools, such as the University of Michigan. For a smaller school that mainly offers undergraduate degrees, Americans usually say 'college,' and people often say 'college' even for a university in casual talk, as in 'Where did you go to college?' In everyday speech, 'school' is also common, as in 'I'm starting school in the fall.'

distinctions.note: In American usage, 'college' often means an undergraduate institution or a school within a university, while 'university' usually means a larger institution offering graduate programs.
'School' is the everyday word for any level of education, and in the US it also covers K-12; 'university' refers specifically to higher education.

examples.everyday: My nephew just got into a university in Texas, so the whole family is excited.
examples.professional: The university partnership gives our data science team access to research computing and graduate interns.
examples.analytical: The modern university has become a place of research, training and credentialing, which shapes what knowledge counts as useful.

nuance.analogy: A university is like a workshop for the mind, where people learn the tools of a discipline and sometimes invent new ones.
nuance.etymology: From Latin universitas, 'the whole, a corporation of teachers and students', from universus 'whole'.
common_mistakes: Using 'college' and 'university' interchangeably; a small undergraduate school is usually called a college, even if it is named a university elsewhere.
Stressing the first syllable as in 'YOO-nih-vur-suh-tee'; the stress belongs on VUR: yoo-nih-VUR-suh-tee.

university.etymology: From Middle English *universite* (“institution of higher learning, body of persons constituting a university”) from Anglo-Norman *université*, from Old French *universitei*, from Medieval Latin stem of *universitas*, in juridical and Late Latin "a number…

senses.definition: Not physically able to be moved.
senses.example: The old oak stump was unmovable, so the crew built the road around it.

senses.definition: Incapable of being emotionally moved or persuaded.
senses.example: Our manager stayed unmovable on the budget, no matter how hard we argued.

core.definition: Impossible to move physically, or too firm in one's position or feelings to be changed or persuaded.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on MOO, the first syllable of the root. The final syllable is a reduced buhl, not 'bull' with a strong vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It describes firmness, which can be admired as resolve or criticized as stubbornness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans usually say immovable for both physical and figurative senses, as in 'an immovable object' or 'immovable on the issue.' Unmovable is accepted and occurs in writing, but it is less common and may sound slightly old-fashioned or literary. In conversation, a natural phrase is 'She's not budging,' or 'He won't change his mind.'

distinctions.note: Immovable is the more common American form in both physical and figurative senses; unmovable is an acceptable alternative with the same meaning.
Unmoved describes someone not emotionally affected at a particular moment; unmovable describes a fixed or stubborn state.

examples.everyday: My grandmother's recliner is unmovable, so we just rearranged the room around it.
examples.professional: The vendor's position on the contract is unmovable, so we need to decide whether to accept the terms.
examples.analytical: If a moral principle is treated as unmovable, the argument shifts from reasons to authority, which deserves scrutiny.

nuance.analogy: Like a boulder in the middle of a path: some people treat their opinions the same way, and no amount of pushing shifts them.
nuance.etymology: From un- (not) plus movable, from Latin movere (to move), via Old French movable.
common_mistakes: Using unmovable in everyday American speech where immovable is more natural.
Mispronouncing the middle syllable, as in 'un-MOV-uh-buhl.'
Assuming unmovable and immovable differ in meaning; they are usually interchangeable.

senses.definition: To remove or retract (something previously posted, such as an electronic message).

core.definition: To remove a post, message, photo, or other content that was previously published online.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on POHST, the second syllable. The final t is a clear, released t, with no vowel after it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; sometimes implies embarrassment, regret, or a response to criticism.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say unpost mainly about social media and online forums, as in I unposted the photo after people complained. It is informal and used most often by younger users or in technical online writing. People often say delete or take down instead, especially for websites, while unpost suggests removing something you posted yourself.

distinctions.note: Delete removes content completely, often permanently; unpost can mean taking a post down while the account stays active.
Retract is more formal and often used for statements or claims, while unpost is informal and used for online content.

examples.everyday: I unposted that picture because my aunt thought it was too embarrassing.
examples.professional: Please unpost the draft announcement from the company page until legal has approved the wording.
examples.analytical: Once a message has been unposted, the question remains whether its earlier circulation can truly be undone.

nuance.analogy: Like taking a flyer off a community bulletin board after everyone has already read it.
nuance.etymology: From un- (reversing an action) and post, to put up a notice, from Latin postis, doorpost.
common_mistakes: Using unpost as a noun, as in an unpost; say a removed post or delete the post.
Confusing unpost with unposed, which describes a natural photo rather than removing online content.

senses.definition: Not realistic.
senses.example: The project timeline was unrealistic given our small team and tight budget.

core.definition: Not based on what is practical or likely; unlikely to be achieved, or not matching real conditions.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on LIS, not on the first syllable of 'real'. Say the 'ea' in 'real' as a weak 'ee-uh', so the word is 'uhn-ree-uh-LIS-tik'.

nuance.connotation: Negative when describing plans, goals or expectations, because it suggests a failure to account for reality.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'That deadline is unrealistic' or 'Your expectations are unrealistic' in meetings, families and everyday conversations. It is more polite than 'That's crazy' or 'You're delusional'. In casual speech, people often shorten it to 'That's not realistic.'

distinctions.note: Impractical means it will not work well in practice, while unrealistic means it does not match reality or expectations.
Unlikely is about probability; unrealistic is about whether a plan or expectation is reasonable.
Idealistic describes hopeful, principled thinking; unrealistic describes failing to account for what is achievable.

examples.everyday: Working out every day for a month is unrealistic for me right now with the kids' schedules.
examples.professional: The launch date is unrealistic, given how much testing we still need to finish.
examples.analytical: A model that assumes perfectly independent samples rests on an unrealistic premise about real-world data.

nuance.analogy: An unrealistic plan is like a map that leaves out the rivers and mountains, so it looks easy but fails on the ground.
nuance.etymology: From un- 'not' plus realistic, from real, from Latin realis 'actual'.
common_mistakes: Putting the stress on the first syllable of 'real' rather than on LIS.
Confusing 'unrealistic' with 'unreal', which means fake, imaginary or dreamlike.
patterns: it is unrealistic to expect sth

senses.definition: Feeling or showing no sorrow or regret for wrongdoing.

core.definition: Not sorry for doing something wrong; showing no guilt, regret, or intention to change.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on PEN, and the first and last syllables are reduced. Americans say the 'r' clearly and do not pronounce the middle 'en' as a separate long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative: it describes someone who shows no remorse for wrongdoing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'unrepentant' mainly for people who have done something clearly wrong and refuse to apologize: 'He was unrepentant about the lie.' It is often used in news and moral discussions. In casual speech, people may say 'he's not even sorry' or 'no remorse.'

distinctions.note: 'Impenitent' is a more formal and religious term; 'unrepentant' is more common in everyday and news English.
'Unapologetic' means not apologizing; 'unrepentant' adds the idea of not feeling regret.

examples.everyday: My cousin is still unrepentant about backing into my mailbox.
examples.professional: The manager was unrepentant after the audit, so the board asked for a formal review.
examples.analytical: Augustine distinguishes the unrepentant heart from the contrite one, since only the latter seeks forgiveness.

nuance.analogy: Like a driver who gets a ticket and says the speed limit was wrong: he has made the mistake, but he does not feel it.
nuance.etymology: From un- plus repentant, from Latin paenitere, 'to be sorry'.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'unrepentance', which is a noun and less common.
Using it for mild regret; it implies a lack of remorse for a real wrong.

senses.definition: Not spoken; not said.
Not formally articulated or stated; implicit or understood.
senses.example: The unspoken rule is to start a new pot of coffee when it is empty.

core.definition: Not said out loud or openly stated; understood by everyone without being expressed in words.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on SPOKE, the second syllable. The final -en is a weak 'kun', not a full 'ken' vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can describe positive shared understanding (unspoken respect) or negative tension (unspoken anger).
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it in everyday and professional speech about rules, feelings, and agreements, as in 'there is an unspoken rule'. It is natural in casual and workplace conversation. Do not confuse it with unspeakable, which means too terrible to describe.

distinctions.note: Implicit is more technical and means contained within something without being stated, while unspoken is about what people leave unsaid.
Tacit is slightly more formal and often used in professional or legal settings for understood but unwritten agreements.
Unsaid is more neutral and may mean simply not mentioned, while unspoken suggests a deliberate or socially shared understanding.

examples.everyday: There's an unspoken rule in our house that whoever cooks doesn't have to do the dishes.
examples.professional: We have an unspoken agreement that the on-call engineer can skip standup, but nobody has written it down.
examples.analytical: Much of the power of the text lies in its unspoken assumptions about who counts as a neighbor.

nuance.analogy: Like a shared map of a city that nobody printed: everyone follows the same routes without a sign.
nuance.etymology: Past participle of speak, from Old English specan, with the negative prefix un-.
common_mistakes: Confusing unspoken with unspeakable, which means too awful to describe.
Pronouncing the ending as a full 'ken'; it is a reduced 'kun'.

senses.definition: Not supportive.
senses.example: His boss was unsupportive when I asked for time off to care for my mother.

core.definition: Not giving encouragement, help, or emotional backing to someone.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on PORT, and the -ive ending is a short, reduced 'iv'. Keep the r clear and the 'or' vowel round, not 'ah'.

nuance.connotation: Negative, and a serious charge when used about a person's attitude toward you.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it about bosses, family members, partners, and friends: 'My manager has been unsupportive about the schedule change.' In casual talk, 'not supportive' is often heard too. Calling someone unsupportive is a strong statement, so a gentler line like 'I feel like you're not fully behind me on this' is more common in personal conversations.

distinctions.note: Unsupportive describes a lack of emotional or moral backing; unhelpful describes practical assistance that is not given.
Unsupportive describes a person's attitude; unsupported describes a claim or position lacking evidence or backing.

examples.everyday: My sister was pretty unsupportive when I said I wanted to switch careers.
examples.professional: Her manager was unsupportive of the new process, so the team stopped using it after two months.
examples.analytical: The critique is unsupportive in tone, yet it offers no alternative for the policy it rejects.

nuance.analogy: Like a coach who only shouts that you are doing it wrong and never offers a hand.
nuance.etymology: From un- (not) plus supportive, from support, from Latin supportare, 'to carry, bring to'.
common_mistakes: Using 'unsupportive' for claims or arguments; for evidence, the word is 'unsupported'.
Stressing the last syllable; the main stress is on PORT: un-suh-PORT-iv.

senses.definition: Not sustainable.
senses.example: Burning fossil fuels at this rate is simply unsustainable for the planet.

senses.definition: Something that cannot be sustained.
senses.example: Managers finally admitted that the unsustainable could not continue much longer.

core.definition: Unable to continue at the current rate or level without running out or causing harm, such as debt, resources, or practices.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on STAY, and the -able ending reduces to 'uh-bul'. Avoid stressing SUS, and do not say the vowel of 'stain' in 'sus-TAIN'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it signals a problem that needs to be fixed.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use unsustainable heavily in business, politics, climate talk and personal finance: 'unsustainable debt' or 'an unsustainable pace.' It is slightly formal but common in everyday news. Saying 'that pace is unsustainable' to a coworker sounds natural. For something merely hard, say exhausting or hard to keep up.

distinctions.note: Unstable describes lack of firmness; unsustainable describes a rate or practice that cannot last over time.
Unaffordable concerns money you cannot pay; unsustainable concerns whether something can continue, including for the environment or a business.

examples.everyday: We can't keep eating out every night, because the budget is just unsustainable.
examples.professional: The current maintenance cost is unsustainable, so we need to cut the backlog this quarter.
examples.analytical: A model of economic growth that ignores resource limits is unsustainable in principle, not merely in practice.

nuance.analogy: Like sprinting at full speed and expecting to keep that pace for a marathon.
nuance.etymology: From un- plus sustainable, from Latin sustinere, to hold up.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as in 'SUS-tain-able'
Using it for something that is only difficult; it means it cannot continue over time

senses.definition: False; not true.
senses.example: She says that I stole her necklace, but that's completely untrue.

senses.definition: Not faithful or loyal.
senses.example: He was untrue to his wife for years, and she finally found out.

core.definition: False or incorrect; not in agreement with what is actually the case.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, TROO. The un- is short and weak, and the vowel in true is a long oo, not a short u.

nuance.connotation: Negative; calling something untrue suggests deception or inaccuracy, and it can sound stiff next to not true or false.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech people usually say that's not true or that's false. Untrue is more common in formal writing, and in the sense of not faithful it sounds literary or old-fashioned, as in untrue to his promises. It works well when you want a careful, slightly formal way to say something is wrong.

distinctions.note: False is direct and common, meaning not factually correct or deliberately deceptive; untrue is more formal and can also mean disloyal.
Untruthful describes a person who does not tell the truth; untrue describes a statement or idea that is not correct.
Inaccurate describes details that are slightly wrong, often by mistake; untrue implies the statement does not match reality at all.

examples.everyday: Don't believe that rumor about Mark, because it's totally untrue.
examples.professional: The first draft of the incident report contained several claims that turned out to be untrue, so we rewrote it.
examples.analytical: A proposition is untrue when it fails to correspond to the facts it describes, a standard that correspondence theories of truth make explicit.

nuance.analogy: Calling a statement untrue is like using a map that does not match the territory: the drawing may look neat, but the roads are not where it says they are.
nuance.etymology: From un- (not) + true, from Old English treowe 'faithful, true'.
common_mistakes: Using untrue as a noun for a lie; the noun is untruth or lie.
Confusing untrue with untruthful; a statement is untrue, but a person is untruthful.

untrue.etymology: From Middle English *untrewe*, from Old English *untrīewe*, from **untriuwī*, from Proto-Germanic **untriwwiz*.

senses.definition: Not yet confirmed; not verified.

core.definition: Not yet checked or confirmed as true, accurate or official.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on VER, the second syllable. Keep the r clear, and pronounce the -ied ending as one syllable that sounds like 'fyde', rhyming with side.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative. It signals caution about information rather than judging it false.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this in news, workplace updates and everyday conversation to say that something has been reported but not confirmed, as in 'The unverified report says the store is closing.' It is careful and neutral, and it keeps you from repeating a rumor as fact. In casual speech, people might say 'I haven't confirmed it' or 'that's just a rumor'.

distinctions.note: Unconfirmed and unverified are close, but unconfirmed often means an official source has not yet approved or announced something, while unverified means the facts have not been checked.
Unverified means not yet checked, and it might still be checked later, while unverifiable means it cannot be checked at all.

examples.everyday: I heard the store is closing, but that's unverified, so let's not panic yet.
examples.professional: Please don't forward the unverified numbers from the vendor until finance has confirmed them.
examples.analytical: The essay relies on unverified eyewitness testimony, so its historical claims remain provisional rather than established.

nuance.analogy: Like a note passed in class before the teacher has read it: you have it, but you have not confirmed what it says.
nuance.etymology: From un- plus verified, from verify, from Medieval Latin verificare 'to make true'.
common_mistakes: Using unverified as a synonym for false; it only means that the information has not been checked.
Stressing the first syllable, saying UN-ver-ified, instead of stressing VER in the second syllable.

senses.definition: In an unworthy manner.

core.definition: In a way that does not deserve respect, honor, or the value someone or something should receive.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on WUR. The th is voiced, as in 'worthy,' and the final -ly is a short 'lee' sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it judges an action as falling short of what is deserved or proper.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly use this adverb in formal writing, sermons, reviews, or literary prose. In casual conversation they say 'unfairly' or 'shamefully' instead. It often appears in phrases like 'treated unworthily' or 'honored unworthily,' which imply that someone received more or less than they deserved.

distinctions.note: Shamefully implies disgrace and strong moral outrage; unworthily describes a failure to match a standard of value or respect.
Unfairly describes injustice in treatment; unworthily describes an action or person failing to fit what is deserved or fitting.

examples.everyday: He treated his brother unworthily after the divorce, and everyone in the family noticed.
examples.professional: We cannot let the team's hard work be unworthily credited to someone who did not write the code.
examples.analytical: Paul warns that whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily is guilty concerning the body and blood of the Lord.

nuance.analogy: Like a fine painting hung in a dark closet, an unworthily treated thing fails to receive the honor its value deserves.
nuance.etymology: From un- (not) plus worthily, from worthy, from Old English weorth, meaning worth or value.
common_mistakes: Using it as a synonym for 'unfairly' in everyday speech; it sounds too formal for ordinary complaints.
Mispronouncing the th as unvoiced (as in 'thin') instead of voiced (as in 'there').
nuance.biblical_note: In the RSV 1 Corinthians 11:27 warns that whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner is guilty, and the Greek word anaxios, meaning unworthily, is the adverb behind this. 1 Corinthians 11:29 explains that the person who eats and drinks without discerning the body is eating judgment on himself. Ephesians 4:1 uses the positive side of the same family, urging readers to lead a life worthy of their calling.

traditions.view: Orthodox Christians prepare for Holy Communion with prayer, fasting, and confession, because receiving unworthily is seen as a serious spiritual danger.
Catholics teach that anyone conscious of grave sin should first receive the sacrament of reconciliation before receiving Communion, so that they do not receive unworthily.

Lutheran and Reformed Protestants usually read the warning as calling for faith and self-examination, while Baptists and many memorialists understand the Lord's Supper as remembrance and read unworthy reception mainly as contempt for the meal.

senses.definition: Not worthy; lacking value or merit; worthless.
senses.example: Critics argued that the senator was unworthy of the office, given his repeated failures to show up.

senses.definition: An inadequate person.
senses.example: Her manager dismissed him as an unworthy who could never finish a project on time.

core.definition: Not deserving of something, or not good enough in value, character, or quality.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on WUR, which uses the American r-colored vowel. The final syllable is a light 'thee' sound, and the 'th' is voiced as in 'this'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It judges someone or something as lacking value or merit, and can sound harsh when applied to people.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'unworthy' most often in formal, moral, or religious contexts, as in 'unworthy of trust.' In casual speech, 'not good enough' or 'doesn't deserve it' are more common. Calling a person 'unworthy' can sound judgmental, so use it with care.

distinctions.note: Worthless means having no value at all; unworthy means not deserving something, which can be a judgment about character or fit.
Undeserving focuses on not earning something; unworthy can also describe a lack of quality or moral standing.

examples.everyday: That movie was unworthy of all the hype, honestly.
examples.professional: The vendor's support record is unworthy of a renewal, so I recommend we look for alternatives.
examples.analytical: Paul warns that anyone who eats the bread or drinks the cup in an unworthy manner is guilty of the body and blood of the Lord, a warning about how the rite is approached.

nuance.analogy: An unworthy object is like a coin that is too worn to spend: it still exists, but it no longer carries the value it should.
nuance.etymology: From Old English 'unwierthe' (not worthy), from 'un-' (not) plus 'worthy.'
common_mistakes: Using 'unworthy' with the wrong preposition: say 'unworthy of' rather than 'unworthy for' or 'unworthy to.'
Using 'unworthy' to mean 'worthless' in casual contexts, which can sound too harsh.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Bible, 'worthy' often translates Greek 'axios' (worthy, deserving). Matthew 10:38 says that whoever does not take up his cross and follow Jesus is not worthy of him. 1 Corinthians 11:27 warns about taking the Lord's supper in an unworthy manner, which calls believers to examine themselves. Matthew 10:37 says that anyone who loves father or mother more than Jesus is not worthy of him.

senses.definition: Not helpful to users; difficult for an untrained person to use.

core.definition: Hard for an untrained person to use, and not helpful to users.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on FREN in 'unfriendly,' and the prefix 'un-' is weak, so it sounds like 'un,' not 'oon.' Keep the 'r' in 'user' and 'friendly' clear and rhotic.

nuance.connotation: Negative, but milder than 'user-hostile.' It is a plain criticism of a design.
nuance.usage_note: Many Americans find 'user-unfriendly' a little awkward, and they more often say 'not very user-friendly' or 'user-hostile' in technical settings. In everyday speech, 'hard to use' or 'confusing' is natural. The phrase is most common in software reviews and IT discussions.

distinctions.note: User-hostile sounds stronger and more pointed, while user-unfriendly is milder and less idiomatic.
'Not user-friendly' has the same meaning but sounds more natural in everyday American English.
Unfriendly describes a person's attitude, while user-unfriendly describes how hard a product is to operate.

examples.everyday: The town's parking app is kind of user-unfriendly, so I usually just pay with cash.
examples.professional: The first version of the form was user-unfriendly, so we rewrote the instructions and cut the number of steps.
examples.analytical: A system that is merely technically correct can still be user-unfriendly when its logic remains hidden from the people who must rely on it.

nuance.analogy: Like a recipe written in a language you cannot read: the steps exist, but they do not help you cook.
nuance.etymology: A compound of 'user' (from 'use') and 'unfriendly,' from Old English 'un-' (not) and 'friendly.'
common_mistakes: Writing 'user unfriendly' without a hyphen before a noun; the hyphen is standard.
Confusing it with 'unfriendly' for a person, as in saying a coworker is 'user-unfriendly' when you mean he is rude.

senses.definition: A person who loans money to others and charges interest, particularly at an exorbitant, exploitative, or illegal rate.

core.definition: A person who lends money at excessive, exploitative, or illegal interest rates, taking advantage of borrowers who have no other choice.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, then say the middle sound like the 's' in 'measure' (zh). The final '-er' is a weak, reduced syllable, so do not say 'you-ser-ER' or 'you-zure-ur' with equal stress.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. Calling someone a usurer condemns them as greedy and predatory, and the word is rarely used neutrally.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly meet this word in historical writing, religious or literary texts, and formal commentary on predatory lending. In everyday talk they usually say 'loan shark' for an illegal lender who uses threats, or 'payday lender' for a legal short-term lender with very high fees. Using 'usurer' in conversation sounds bookish but is understood immediately.

distinctions.note: A loan shark is an informal, usually illegal lender who uses intimidation to collect, while a usurer is a formal term for anyone charging exploitative interest, legal or not.
Moneylender is a neutral, sometimes legal term for anyone who lends money for interest, with no implication of exploitation.
Creditor is the neutral term for anyone you owe money to, and it carries no moral judgment at all.

examples.everyday: My cousin got a loan from some company online, and the interest is insane, so I told him that lender is basically a usurer.
examples.professional: Compliance flagged one of our partner lenders as a usurer because its fees far exceeded state limits on consumer loans.
examples.analytical: Medieval theologians condemned the usurer not merely for charging interest but for selling time, which they regarded as belonging to God alone.

nuance.analogy: A usurer is like a fishhook that is easy to swallow but hard to get out of, since the borrower is drawn in by the loan and then caught by the rising debt.
nuance.etymology: From Old French usurier, from Latin usura (use, interest), from usus, the past participle of uti (to use).
common_mistakes: Confusing 'usurer' with 'usurper', which means someone who seizes power or rights unlawfully.
Pronouncing it as 'you-SURE-er' with stress on the second syllable; the stress is on the first syllable.
Using 'usurer' as a neutral word for any lender in everyday conversation, when it is a strong insult.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Hebrew Scriptures, lending at interest to a fellow Israelite in need is forbidden. The Hebrew words are neshek (literally 'bite', the idea of interest biting into the debtor) and tarbit ('increase'). Exodus 22:25 forbids charging interest to a poor fellow Israelite, Leviticus 25:36-37 forbids taking interest or increase from a brother in need, and Deuteronomy 23:19-20 permits charging interest to a foreigner but not to a brother. The prohibition is focused on exploitation of the poor within the covenant community.

traditions.view: Orthodox canon law historically condemned usury, especially for clergy, and Orthodox ethical teaching has treated exploitative lending as a serious sin against neighbor and justice.
The Church historically prohibited usury as an injustice, and modern Catholic teaching condemns exploitative lending while accepting fair interest on legitimate loans.
Martin Luther condemned usury, while John Calvin accepted moderate interest on commercial loans; Lutheran and Reformed Protestants have differed on how strictly to apply the biblical prohibition.

senses.definition: Any subordinate bound by similar close ties.
senses.example: Their company treated each small supplier as a vassal of the larger parent firm.

senses.definition: (historical) Any direct subordinate bound by such vows to a superior.
senses.example: The king ordered his vassals to join him on the crusade unless they had a written note signed by the archbishop or pope.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (historical) The grantee of a fief, a subordinate granted use of a superior's land and its income in exchange for vows of fidelity and homage and (typically) military service.
senses.example: The manor's vassals owed first fruits and a tithe to the parish church, another 10% to the lord (including at least 50 eels), a week or two each year of service in the manor's upkeep, and service in the local fyrd.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: Resembling a vassal; slavish; servile.
senses.example: His vassal attitude toward the senator made the staff uncomfortable during every meeting.

senses.definition: To treat as a vassal or to reduce to the position of a vassal; to subject to control; to enslave.
senses.example: The conquering army vassaled the border towns, demanding tribute and loyalty every single year.

senses.definition: To subordinate to someone or something.
senses.example: Our church should not vassal its ministry to any political party or donor.

core.definition: In medieval Europe, a man who held land from a lord in exchange for loyalty, homage and military service.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the word is two syllables with a short a as in 'cat'. Learners often say 'VESS-ul', which is the word for a container, so keep the a sound short and open.

nuance.connotation: Negative in most uses, since it suggests dependence, servitude or lack of independence.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly for medieval feudal relationships in history classes and books, and it is occasionally used figuratively for someone who is dependent or subservient. Calling a coworker or friend a vassal is an insult, so use it with care. In everyday talk, people more often say 'underling' or 'subordinate'.

distinctions.note: A serf was tied to the land and worked it for a lord, while a vassal was typically a free noble or knight holding a fief through an oath.
Subordinate is a neutral workplace word, while vassal is historical and carries a strong sense of dependence and servitude.

examples.everyday: My friend joked that at work he is basically a vassal, always waiting for the boss to give orders.
examples.professional: Our small company is essentially a vassal of the parent corporation, since it must approve every budget.
examples.analytical: Medieval vassals owed military service to their lords, but the bond was personal and reciprocal rather than a modern contract.

nuance.analogy: A vassal is like a branch office that holds its territory from headquarters, owes it loyalty and support, and can be overruled from above.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin vassallus, servant, probably from a Celtic word meaning servant or youth.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like 'vessel', with an e vowel instead of a short a.
Using vassal as a neutral word for employee; it implies dependence and servitude.

vassal.etymology: From Middle English *vassal*, from Old French *vassal*, from Medieval Latin *vassallus* (“manservant, domestic, retainer”), from Latin *vassus* (“servant”), from **wassos* (“young man, squire”), from **wastos* (“servant”).

senses.definition: A way of life which strictly avoids animal products and services involving the use of living animals.
senses.example: She adopted veganism after watching a documentary about factory farming in Iowa.

senses.definition: Strict vegetarianism; the practice of eating neither meat nor other animal products, such as fish, milk and milk products, eggs, and honey.
senses.example: My brother's veganism means he skips eggs, butter, and even honey in his baking.

core.definition: A way of life and diet that avoids all animal products, including meat, dairy, eggs and honey, and often animal-tested goods.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, VEE. The middle syllable is reduced to 'guh', and the ending is a reduced 'iz-um', not 'izm' with a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive for supporters; some people see it as preachy or political, so it can sound charged in debate.
nuance.usage_note: Americans usually say 'I'm vegan' in conversation and reserve veganism for discussing the philosophy or movement. Strict vegans avoid honey, leather and other animal-derived goods, which people may not expect, so ask before serving food. Plant-based is more common in product marketing and is not the same as vegan.

distinctions.note: Vegetarianism excludes meat and fish, but many vegetarians still eat eggs, dairy or honey; veganism excludes all animal products.
Plant-based describes a diet centered on plants and does not always rule out animal products; vegan is stricter.

examples.everyday: My sister switched to veganism last year, so she always asks about the ingredients in restaurant dishes.
examples.professional: The catering menu lists vegan options, so we should add a dietary question about veganism to the RSVP form.
examples.analytical: Veganism is best understood as a moral position about animal use rather than merely a diet, which is why its supporters often focus on ethics.

nuance.analogy: Veganism is like a no-animal-products rule that applies to clothing and daily purchases, not only to the dinner table.
nuance.etymology: Coined in 1944 by Donald Watson from the first three and last two letters of vegetarian.
common_mistakes: Mixing up veganism with vegetarianism when describing what someone eats.
Using veganism as a verb; say 'to be vegan' or 'to go vegan'.
Assuming vegans avoid only meat; in practice they also avoid dairy, eggs and honey.

senses.definition: Covered by a veil.
senses.example: The bride walked slowly down the aisle, veiled in soft white lace.

senses.definition: Partly hidden or concealed.
senses.example: veiled threats

core.definition: Partly hidden or disguised, so that the real meaning is not stated directly, as in a veiled threat.

pronunciation.tip: The word is one syllable, pronounced like 'sailed'. Do not add an extra vowel or say 'vee-uld', even though the spelling begins with ve.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It usually suggests that someone is hiding a real meaning, often a threat or criticism.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use it in phrases like 'a veiled threat' or 'a veiled criticism.' It is more common in news, writing and serious conversation than in casual speech. In literal contexts, it can describe a face or a woman wearing a veil.

distinctions.note: Hidden means not visible at all, while veiled means partly visible or implied, so the true meaning can be guessed.
Implicit is a neutral word for something understood without being stated, while veiled usually suggests the speaker intends to hide a point.

examples.everyday: He made a veiled comment about my cooking, and everyone at the table got uncomfortable.
examples.professional: Her email included a veiled warning that the team might leave if nothing changed by the end of the quarter.
examples.analytical: The author's veiled critique of the institution becomes visible only when the essay is read against the sermons it quotes.

nuance.analogy: A veiled meaning is like a face seen through a thin curtain: you can see the shape, but not the details.
nuance.etymology: From veil, from Old French voile, from Latin velum, covering or sail.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'vield' or 'veeld' rather than 'vayld'.
Using veiled to mean secret in general, when it specifically suggests a partly open hint or indirect message.

senses.definition: The art of projecting one's voice without moving the lips so that it appears to come from another source, such as a dummy.

core.definition: The art of speaking without moving your lips so that your voice seems to come from another place, such as a puppet.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, TRIL. The 'o' is a reduced vowel in standard American speech, so the middle sounds like 'uh,' not 'oh.' The final syllable is a weak 'um.'

nuance.connotation: Positive or playful: it is associated with entertainment, comedy and performance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ventriloquism mostly for stage shows, television and children's entertainment. The person is a ventriloquist, and the puppet is usually called a dummy in traditional talk. Americans rarely use the word for ordinary voice imitation, which they call mimicry.

distinctions.note: Mimicry imitates other voices openly; ventriloquism makes the voice seem to come from another source.
Voice acting gives a character a voice in recordings; ventriloquism hides the speaker's mouth movements.

examples.everyday: My cousin does ventriloquism at birthday parties, and the kids love the talking duck.
examples.professional: The conference keynote opened with a short ventriloquism routine to show how audiences trust what they hear.
examples.analytical: Ventriloquism depends on what psychologists call the ventriloquist effect, in which we locate a voice where our eyes see movement.

nuance.analogy: Ventriloquism is like a magic trick for the ears: the sound seems to come from the puppet, while the real speaker stays hidden.
nuance.etymology: From Latin venter, belly, and loqui, to speak, so literally speaking from the belly.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle vowel as oh, as in 'ven-tri-LOH-kwizm.'
Calling the person a ventriloquism when the correct word is ventriloquist.

senses.definition: A person, especially an entertainer, who practices ventriloquism.
senses.example: The ventriloquist made the wooden dummy seem to argue with the audience at the county fair.

core.definition: A performer who makes his or her voice seem to come from a puppet or another source without moving the lips.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TRIL, and the first syllable is ven, not vent. Americans reduce the middle syllables to uh, and the -quist ends with a clear s and t.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it describes an entertainer, often with a sense of fun.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ventriloquist for stage and TV performers, especially those with a puppet called a dummy. Many performers use dummy casually, though some prefer puppet. Calling an ordinary speaker a ventriloquist is rare and humorous.

distinctions.note: A puppeteer moves the puppet visibly; a ventriloquist speaks for it while keeping the mouth still.
An impressionist imitates other people's voices openly; a ventriloquist makes the voice seem to come from elsewhere.

examples.everyday: We saw a ventriloquist at the county fair, and my daughter laughed the whole time.
examples.professional: Our marketing team hired a ventriloquist for the product launch, and it got everyone's attention.
examples.analytical: A ventriloquist asks the audience to believe that the puppet, not the performer, is speaking.

nuance.analogy: Like a ghostwriter for a voice: the words come from one person, but the audience hears them from another place.
nuance.etymology: From Latin venter, meaning belly, and loqui, meaning to speak.
common_mistakes: Adding a t after the n; the first syllable is ven, not vent.
Stressing the middle syllable; say ven-TRIL-uh-kwist, with the stress on TRIL.

senses.definition: The series of vertebrae that protect the spinal cord; the spinal column.

core.definition: The spine: the chain of vertebrae that surrounds and protects the spinal cord.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on KAH in 'column', with a light secondary stress on 'vur'. 'Column' is pronounced with a short 'ah' vowel, not a long 'o'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and clinical. It is used in medicine and anatomy rather than casual talk.
nuance.usage_note: Doctors, nurses, and anatomy textbooks use this term, and a patient may see it on an X-ray report or a physical therapy note. In everyday American speech people say 'spine' or 'backbone'. Using 'vertebral column' in casual conversation can sound clinical.

distinctions.note: 'Spine' is the everyday word for the same structure, while 'vertebral column' is the precise anatomical term used in medicine and science.
The spinal cord is the nerve tissue inside the column, while the vertebral column is the bony structure that surrounds and protects it.

collocations: the vertebral column of a fish

examples.everyday: My doctor said the X-ray shows my vertebral column is fine, so the pain is probably muscular.
examples.professional: The insurance form asks for a description of any injury to the vertebral column.
examples.analytical: The vertebral column is segmented, and that segmentation lets the body bend and rotate while protecting the spinal cord.

nuance.analogy: The vertebral column is like a stack of spools on a rod, with a hollow channel down the middle that carries the cord.
nuance.etymology: From Latin vertebra 'joint, vertebra', from vertere 'to turn'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'vertebrate column', since 'vertebrate' means an animal with a backbone, not the spine itself
Pronouncing 'column' as 'KOH-lum' with a long o instead of KAH-lum

senses.definition: A political right to disapprove of (and thereby stop) the process of a decision, a law etc.
senses.example: The governor used her veto to block the controversial tax bill passed by the legislature.

senses.definition: An invocation of that right.
An authoritative prohibition or negative; a forbidding; an interdiction.
senses.example: Her parents' veto on late-night parties ended any hope of a sleepover.

senses.definition: A technique or mechanism for discarding what would otherwise constitute a false positive in a scientific experiment.
senses.example: The analysis pipeline used a veto on signals that failed the secondary detector cross-check.

senses.definition: To use a veto against.
senses.example: The president vetoed the bill.

senses.definition: To countermand.
senses.example: Mom and Dad vetoed our menu preferences for the holiday meal.

core.definition: Noun: the official right to reject a decision or law. Verb: to reject or block a decision using that right, or to forbid something firmly.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, VEE. The second syllable is a clear, long oh sound, so do not reduce it to a schwa.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. A veto blocks something, so it can be frustrating to the people affected, though it may be seen as a necessary check.
nuance.usage_note: In American politics, veto is standard in news and civic discussion, especially for presidents and governors. In everyday speech, people use it jokingly for a family or group decision, as in my wife vetoed the idea. Saying I veto that to a friend is a playful way to reject a plan.

distinctions.note: Reject is a general word for refusing something. Veto is more formal and implies an official right or power to block.
To override is to pass a measure again despite a veto. Veto is the initial rejection; override is the response.

examples.everyday: My wife vetoed the camping trip in January, so we're going to a hotel instead.
examples.professional: Legal can veto the launch if the new feature raises privacy concerns, so we should check with them first.
examples.analytical: The veto is a check on majority power, but it also concentrates authority in a single office.

nuance.analogy: A veto is like a stop sign at an intersection, blocking movement even if other traffic wants to go.
nuance.etymology: From Latin vetō, I forbid, first person singular of vetare, to forbid.
common_mistakes: Using veto as a noun for a general refusal, when it usually refers to an official or formal power.
Stressing the second syllable as vee-TOH, which is not the standard American pattern.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to a vicar.
Delegated; vicarious.

core.definition: Relating to a vicar, or acting or delegated in place of another person in a church role.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, 'KAIR'. The 'r' is American and should be clear, and the final syllable is weak, not a full 'ul'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise term from church and legal language, not an everyday word.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'vicarial' in conversation. They usually say 'vicarious' for something experienced through another person, or 'pastoral' for a pastor's care. In church settings, 'vicar' is mainly an Anglican term for a parish priest, so 'vicarial' is mostly found in academic or historical writing.

distinctions.note: 'Vicarious' is the everyday word for experiencing something through another person, while 'vicarial' is a rare, church-specific term.
'Pastoral' describes care for a congregation or a pastor's role, while 'vicarial' describes acting on behalf of someone else.

examples.professional: During the bishop's absence, she held vicarial authority over the diocese's financial decisions.
examples.analytical: The claim that the pope holds a vicarial power of Christ is precisely what Eastern Orthodox and many Protestant critics dispute.

nuance.analogy: A vicarial role is like a substitute teacher: they stand in for the person who normally holds the position.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'vicarius', substitute, from 'vicis', change or turn.
common_mistakes: Using 'vicarial' where 'vicarious' is meant, for example 'vicarial experience'.
Pronouncing it 'vik-AIR-ee-ul'; the first vowel is a long 'eye' sound, as in 'vibe'.

traditions.view: The pope is called the Vicar of Christ as successor of Peter, and bishops act as vicars of Christ in their dioceses.
Orthodox theology speaks of bishops as representing Christ in their local churches but rejects the idea that any single bishop is Christ's universal vicar.

Most Protestant churches do not use the vicar concept for ordained ministers; Anglican churches use 'vicar' for a parish priest, while Lutheran and Reformed churches emphasize Christ's direct rule over the church.

senses.definition: Transient visual content or media, processed with technology, especially electronic.
senses.example: Early TV used film to record video.

senses.definition: A recording or medium of visual content, especially audiovisual content for playback; a motion picture, movie, film.
senses.example: We edited a video montage of Robbie's first birthday.

senses.definition: (dated) Television content or media.
senses.example: We had a television set, but the video was mostly reruns of sitcoms.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: (dated) Videotape, VHS.
senses.example: Dad still has a box of old video in the garage, all labeled in his handwriting.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: To visually record (activity, or a motion picture) in general, with or without sound.
senses.example: We video the kids' recital so Grandma can watch it from Florida.

core.definition: A recording of moving images, often with sound, that you can watch on a screen, TV, phone or computer.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and keep the middle 'ee' and final 'oh' as two clear vowels. Do not say 'vi-DAY-oh' or stress the last syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a common, practical medium, and tone depends on the content.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'video' constantly, for personal clips, online content, meetings, movies and recordings. In casual speech, people say 'a video' or 'send me the video'. As a verb, 'to video' is less common than 'to record' or 'to film'. The older sense of 'video' meaning television is now dated.

distinctions.note: Film often refers to a feature-length story made for cinema, while video is a broader term for any recorded moving image.
Clip is a short segment, usually taken from a longer video or movie.
Footage is raw, unedited recorded material, while video is usually a finished or shareable product.

examples.everyday: Let me send you a video of the kids at the recital, they were adorable.
examples.professional: Can you record a short video of the demo so the client can review it asynchronously?
examples.analytical: A video is never a neutral record, because framing, editing and sound shape how viewers interpret the event.

nuance.analogy: A video is like a flipbook made of light: many still pictures shown so quickly that they look like motion.
nuance.etymology: From Latin videre, 'to see', in the first-person form video, 'I see'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable, as in 'vi-DEE-oh'; the main stress is on the first syllable.
Using 'video' as a mass noun in phrases like 'I watched video all day'; in everyday American English, people usually say 'videos' or 'I watched videos'.

video.etymology: From the root vide of Latin *videō* (“to see”) + -o, formed in analogy to *audio*.

senses.definition: (Can we clean up this sense?) A vile, wicked person.
senses.example: Everyone in the village knew the old landlord was a villain who cheated widows.

senses.definition: An extremely depraved person, or one capable or guilty of great crimes.
senses.example: The detective said the serial killer was a villain capable of unspeakable cruelty.

senses.definition: A deliberate scoundrel.
senses.example: The insurance agent turned out to be a villain who had been stealing from clients for years.

senses.definition: A character who has the role of being bad, especially antagonizing the hero; an antagonist who is also evil or malevolent.
senses.example: In the film, the villain delights in stealing the hero's car and tormenting his family.

senses.definition: Any opponent player, especially a hypothetical player for example and didactic purposes. Compare: hero (“the current player”).
senses.example: Let's discuss how to play if you are the chip leader (that is, if you have more chips than all the villains).

core.definition: A wicked person, especially a character in a story, film or play who opposes the hero and does evil deeds.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on VIL, and the second syllable is a reduced, unstressed schwa, so it sounds like 'un', not 'ane'. The dictionary's '.' in the IPA is a syllable break, not a stress mark, so no extra stress is needed on the second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative, though it can be used playfully. In everyday talk, people use it jokingly about someone who causes trouble.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say villain most often about movie, TV, and book characters, and they also use it casually for a person who caused a problem, as in 'the villain who ate my leftovers'. In serious news reporting people usually say 'criminal' or 'suspect' instead. Calling a real person a villain is strong and can sound judgmental, so use it with care.

distinctions.note: Bad guy is more casual and common in speech, while villain is slightly more literary and is used especially for fictional antagonists.
A criminal has broken the law, while a villain may be evil in a story or morally wicked without necessarily breaking any law.

examples.everyday: Honestly, the villain in that show is more interesting than the hero.
examples.professional: Our test suite caught the villain of the release, a race condition in the login service.
examples.analytical: Milton's Satan is a villain whose rhetorical power makes his evil seem persuasive.

nuance.analogy: A villain is like the dark spot in a painting that makes the bright colors stand out; the story needs them to show what the hero stands for.
nuance.etymology: From Old French vilain ('farmhand, peasant'), from Medieval Latin villanus, from villa ('farm'); the meaning shifted from peasant to base person to wicked person.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'vil-LAIN', with stress on the second syllable.
Using villain for any unpleasant person in everyday life; it is usually reserved for stories or for strong moral condemnation.

villain.etymology: Probably from Middle English *vilein*, from Old French *vilein*, in turn from Late Latin *vīllānus*, meaning serf or peasant, someone who is bound to the soil of a Latin *vīlla*, which is to say, worked on the equivalent of a plantation in late Antiquity,…

senses.definition: A software agent that can perform tasks and services for an individual.
senses.example: The smart speaker's virtual assistant set a timer and read the weather.

senses.definition: A person employed to provide professional administrative services to clients, working remotely from a home office.
senses.example: I hired a virtual assistant to handle my scheduling and invoices from the Philippines.

core.definition: A software program that understands spoken or typed requests and carries out tasks, such as Siri or Alexa.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on 'SIS' in 'assistant'. In 'virtual', the 't' sounds like 'ch', so it is 'VER-choo-uhl', and the final 'ant' is reduced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and practical. It is positive when the assistant is helpful, but can be frustrating if it misunderstands.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'virtual assistant' for voice-activated programs on phones and smart speakers. It can also mean a remote worker who handles administrative tasks for clients, which is common in small business talk. In casual conversation, people often just say 'Alexa' or 'Siri' rather than the general term.

distinctions.note: A chatbot is usually text-based and may be built for one website, while a virtual assistant often works across several tasks and devices through voice or text.
An executive assistant is usually a person who works in the office, while a virtual assistant can be a remote worker or a software program.

examples.everyday: I asked my virtual assistant to set a timer for the pasta, and it did it right away.
examples.professional: We're piloting a virtual assistant to sort IT tickets before they reach the support team.
examples.analytical: A virtual assistant's apparent understanding is largely statistical pattern matching, not comprehension in the human sense.

nuance.analogy: A virtual assistant is like a digital receptionist who never sleeps and answers instantly.
nuance.etymology: 'Virtual' from Medieval Latin 'virtualis' (having power or effect); 'assistant' from Latin 'assistere' (to stand by).
common_mistakes: Stressing 'virtual' on the second syllable as 'vir-TU-al'; the stress is on 'VER'.
Saying 'virtual assistance' when you mean the program; 'assistance' is the help itself, not the tool.

conversation.text: A virtual assistant helps with tasks like scheduling, reminders, and quick questions, often by voice.
Older virtual assistants handled fixed commands; newer ones can handle open-ended requests.
She works as a virtual assistant, managing email and calendars for three small business owners.

senses.definition: In a vocal manner.
senses.example: Passengers complained long and vocally about the timetable changes.

senses.definition: Using words.
senses.example: The infant responded vocally to the first stimulus in the study.

core.definition: In a loud, open way that uses your voice, often to express support or opposition.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, VOH. The middle syllable is weak, so keep it short and reduced, and end with a clear long E sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It usually describes open, strong statements of support or opposition.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'vocally opposed' or 'vocally supportive' in news, meetings and everyday talk. It is more common in writing and formal speech than in casual chat, where people often say 'really speak up about' or 'loudly.' It describes the manner of expressing something rather than the content.

distinctions.note: Verbally means in words, spoken or written, while vocally emphasizes using the voice and expressing something openly.
Orally means by mouth or spoken rather than written, and is common in exams and medicine.

examples.everyday: My sister is vocally against the new parking rule, and she brings it up at every family dinner.
examples.professional: Two team leads were vocally opposed to the migration plan during the review.
examples.analytical: The reformers were vocally critical of clerical privilege, though their positive program remained ambiguous.

nuance.analogy: Speaking vocally is like turning up the volume on a position so that everyone in the room can hear it.
nuance.etymology: From vocal plus the adverbial suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Confusing vocally with verbally. Use vocally for loud or open expression with the voice.
Pronouncing the first vowel as a short 'o' instead of the long 'oh' sound in VOH.

senses.definition: The state of being volatile.
The state of having a low boiling point and evaporating readily.
senses.example: The volatility of acetone makes it evaporate quickly from an open container.

senses.definition: The state of not retaining data in the absence of power.
senses.example: RAM has volatility, so unsaved data disappears when the laptop loses power.

senses.definition: The state of being able to fly.
The state of being unpredictable.
A quantification of the degree of uncertainty about the future price of a commodity, share, or other financial product.
senses.example: Traders watched the volatility of tech stocks spike after the earnings report.

core.definition: The degree to which a price, market, or situation changes suddenly and unpredictably.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on TIL, with a light secondary stress on the first syllable. Non-native speakers often stress the last syllable or pronounce the middle vowel as a full sound instead of a reduced one.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in technical and chemical contexts; often negative in finance and news when it signals instability and risk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use volatility mostly in finance, economics, and news reporting, as in stock market volatility or a volatile political climate. In casual conversation people usually say the market is unstable or unpredictable instead. In chemistry it describes how readily a liquid evaporates, but that sense is rare outside science classes.

distinctions.note: Instability describes a general lack of steadiness, while volatility refers specifically to sharp, frequent swings in a measurable value such as a price.
Variance is a statistical measure of spread, while in finance volatility is usually the standard deviation of returns, which is the square root of variance.

examples.everyday: I barely check my retirement account anymore because the market's volatility makes me nervous.
examples.professional: Our forecast missed badly because the model did not account for the sudden volatility in energy prices last quarter.
examples.analytical: Volatility measures how widely outcomes disperse around an average, but it says nothing about whether those outcomes are good or bad.

nuance.analogy: Like a weather forecast that swings from sunshine to storm within an hour: the average may look calm, but the swings are sharp.
nuance.etymology: From Latin volatilis, flying, from volare, to fly.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable (vuh-LAT-) instead of TIL.
Using volatility for a person's temper; use the adjective volatile instead, as in a volatile temper.

senses.definition: Reliance on volunteers to perform a social or educational function.
The tendency to volunteer; the activity of volunteering.
senses.example: His volunteerism eventually burned him out.

core.definition: Volunteering as a social practice, and the reliance on unpaid volunteers to provide community services.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on TEER, and the -ism ending reduces to 'ih-zum', not a long 'izm'. Use the American 'ah' vowel in the first syllable, as in 'cot', not 'aw'.

nuance.connotation: Positive: it praises unpaid service that benefits communities.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in civic, nonprofit and academic discussions, as in 'corporate volunteerism' or 'rising youth volunteerism'. Ordinary people usually say 'volunteering' or 'helping out' instead. It can sound abstract, so use it when discussing a trend or culture rather than a single act.

distinctions.note: Volunteering is the act of helping; volunteerism is the broader practice or culture of relying on volunteers.
Philanthropy usually means giving money to good causes; volunteerism means giving time and effort.
A charity is an organization or act of giving to people in need; volunteerism is unpaid service in general.

examples.everyday: Our neighborhood has so much volunteerism that the park gets cleaned up every month.
examples.professional: Our corporate volunteerism program gives employees paid time to tutor kids once a month.
examples.analytical: Scholars debate whether volunteerism builds civic trust or lets the state avoid responsibility for public services.

nuance.analogy: Like a community potluck: everyone brings something, and nobody gets paid for the dish.
nuance.etymology: From volunteer plus -ism, from French volontaire, from Latin voluntarius, 'of one's own will'.
common_mistakes: Confusing volunteerism with volunteering: volunteerism names the broader practice, while volunteering is the act itself.
Pronouncing the first vowel as 'aw', as in 'vawl'; the American vowel is the 'ah' of 'cot'.

senses.definition: Characterized or marked by full, generous, pleasurable sensation.
senses.example: The plentiful blankets and the voluptuous pillows of the bed called out to my tired body.

senses.definition: Curvaceous and sexually attractive.
senses.example: The low neckline of her bodice emphasized her plump, voluptuous figure.

core.definition: Full, curvy, and sexually attractive; also richly pleasing to the senses.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LUHP. The tch is one sound, and the -uous ending is weak, so it sounds like choo-uhs, not two full syllables.

nuance.connotation: Can be positive or negative; as a description of a body it can be admiring but also old-fashioned or objectifying, and in literature it can mean lavish pleasure.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use voluptuous mainly to describe curvy women in a complimentary or literary way, and it can sound dated or objectifying in modern talk. For describing a person, many prefer curvy or full-figured. In writing it can also describe lavish food, music, or rich colors that delight the senses.

distinctions.note: Curvy is common, neutral, and everyday for describing a body shape; voluptuous is more emphatic and can sound dated or sensual.
Luxurious refers to expensive comfort; voluptuous emphasizes sensual fullness and pleasure rather than cost.

examples.everyday: The chocolate cake was so rich and voluptuous that we each took one more bite.
examples.professional: The designer described the fabric as voluptuous, but our store customers asked for something lighter and easier to wash.
examples.analytical: The painter's voluptuous color and texture make the canvas feel physically warm, which is the point of its sensual argument.

nuance.analogy: Like a thick, velvet curtain that fills the room with color and softness: it draws the eye and invites touch.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin voluptuosus, from Latin voluptas, pleasure.
common_mistakes: Using voluptuous to mean voluminous, which means large in quantity.
Stressing the last syllable of the word instead of LUHP.

voluptuous.etymology: From Middle French *voluptueux*, from Latin *voluptuōsus* (“delightful”), from *voluptās* (“pleasure, delight”), from *volup* (“with pleasure”).

senses.definition: Vomit (the product of an emesis).
senses.example: The nurse cleaned the vomitus from the hallway floor before the next patient arrived.

core.definition: Matter that has been vomited; vomit, especially when described in a medical or forensic context.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, VAH, and make the final syllable a weak 'tus', as in 'VAH-mih-tus'. The 'i' in the middle is a short, reduced vowel, not a long 'ee'.

nuance.connotation: Clinical and neutral, but graphic; it is used to describe the material itself rather than the act.
nuance.usage_note: This word is used almost only in medical, nursing, or forensic writing in American English. Ordinary speakers would say 'vomit' and would not use 'vomitus' in conversation. Using it outside clinical settings can sound overly technical or even comic.

distinctions.note: Vomit is the everyday word for the material; vomitus is clinical and mainly used in medical or forensic reports.
Emesis refers to the act of vomiting in technical language, while vomitus refers to the material expelled.

examples.everyday: The nurse asked me to describe the color of the vomitus, so I just said it was yellow and smelled sour.
examples.professional: The triage note records coffee-ground vomitus in the emergency bay, which raises concern for an upper GI bleed.
examples.analytical: The clinical report characterizes the vomitus as bilious, which suggests that the obstruction lies beyond the ampulla of Vater.

nuance.analogy: Like a lab label: the same stuff you would simply call vomit, but written in a form meant for doctors.
nuance.etymology: From Latin vomitus, past participle of vomere 'to vomit'.
common_mistakes: Using it in casual speech, where 'vomit' is the natural word.
Mispronouncing it with a long 'ee' vowel in the middle, as in 'VAH-mee-tus'.

senses.definition: Someone who works for wages and has little to no professional autonomy.
senses.example: I felt like a wage slave, clocking in every morning for a boss who never listened.

senses.definition: Someone who does very unpleasant or drudging work for a wage.
senses.example: Scrubbing dishes for eleven hours at minimum wage, he felt like a wage slave.

core.definition: Someone who depends on a paycheck and has little control over the work or working conditions.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the word 'slave' more than 'wage', and keep 'wage' with a soft 'j' sound. The final 'v' is voiced, so do not replace it with an 'f'.

nuance.connotation: Negative and emotionally sharp. It suggests a person feels trapped or exploited, so it can offend a manager or employer.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use wage slave in casual talk, labor debates, and social media when someone feels overworked or powerless. It is strong language, so avoid using it about your own boss in a professional setting unless you want to start a serious conversation. Historically, the phrase is tied to critiques of wage labor, so people may use it as a political statement.

distinctions.note: Employee is neutral and factual, while wage slave is emotionally loaded and emphasizes lack of freedom.
A workaholic chooses to work long hours, while a wage slave feels forced to work by financial need or fear of losing a job.

examples.everyday: After another double shift, I feel like a wage slave with no time for my own life.
examples.professional: When several team members called the workload wage slave work, we reviewed the schedule and pay with HR.
examples.analytical: Critics of industrial capitalism used the phrase wage slavery to argue that workers sell their labor under conditions they cannot control.

nuance.analogy: Like a rowboat that stays on course only because the rower never stops pulling the oars, with no real choice of direction.
nuance.etymology: Wage (from Old French gage, a pledge) plus slave (from Medieval Latin sclavus, a captive).
common_mistakes: Using wage slave casually about a boss in front of coworkers, where it may sound like an attack.
Confusing wage slave, a figurative complaint about work, with legal slavery, which is a historical and literal condition.

senses.definition: To relinquish (a right etc.); to give up claim to; to forgo.
senses.example: If you waive the right to be silent, anything you say can be used against you in a court of law.

senses.definition: To relinquish claim on a payment or fee which would otherwise be due.
senses.example: The bank agreed to waive the late fee since it was my first mistake.

senses.definition: To release [a player] onto the waiver wire.
senses.example: The Yankees decided to waive the veteran reliever after a poor spring.

senses.definition: (rare) To put aside, avoid.
senses.example: He chose to waive the formalities and get straight to the point.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: To voluntarily give up a right, claim, or requirement, such as a fee or a legal right.
